intro: About 53 questions in about 120 minutes, USD 125 at Pearson VUE; the 720/1000 pass mark comes from the community blueprint, since Anthropic has published no cut score. It tests building on Claude: the Messages API and structured output, model choice and cost, agents, prompts and context, tool use and MCP, security, Claude Code and evals. Read each domain's summary and traps first, watch the video, then drill the notes and flashcards in weight order; a third of the paper is Applications and Integration.

summary.tests: Whether you can wire Claude into real software: stateless Messages API calls, tool-based structured output, CI/CD review, batch jobs and document pipelines with validation, routing and failure handling.
must_know: The Messages API is stateless: resend the full history (with every `tool_use` and `tool_result` block), the system prompt and `max_tokens` on each call.
In CI run `claude -p --output-format json --json-schema`, read `structured_output` and branch on the exit code.
Force structure with a tool schema: `tool_choice` of `any` when the tool varies, a named `tool` to force one; nullable fields stop fabrication.
Batches: 50% cheaper, 100,000 requests or 256 MB, expire at 24 hours (usually under 1 hour), results kept 29 days, match on `custom_id`.
Schema-valid is not correct: read `stop_reason` (`max_tokens`, `refusal`), check business rules, retry with the error fed back, then escalate.
Retry 429, 5xx and 529 with exponential backoff, jitter and `retry-after`; never retry 400-class errors; the SDKs retry twice by default.
Tool failures go back as `tool_result` with `is_error: true`; a PDF is limited to 32 MB and 600 pages per request.
traps: Fixing flaky JSON with regex, louder instructions or temperature instead of a schema plus validation and retry.
Sending a user-facing step through the Batches API (up to 24 hours) or matching batch results by position.
Making every field required so Claude invents team names, ticket ids or dates the document never states.

notes.objective: Integrate Claude into CI/CD pipelines to analyze code submissions and provide structured feedback on pull requests using tool use and the Messages API.
notes.title: Messages API calls are stateless
notes.gist: Every request must carry the whole conversation, so your code owns the history, the system prompt and the exact block structure.
points: Stateless: send the full `messages` history and the `system` prompt on every call; earlier assistant turns may be synthetic, which is how you edit or truncate a conversation.
Replay assistant turns as content blocks, never flattened text: each `tool_use` needs its `tool_result` next, and `thinking` blocks must come back unmodified or the API returns a 400.
`max_tokens` is required; the reply `content` is an array of typed blocks, not a string, and carries `stop_reason` and `usage`.
Return every `tool_result` from one assistant turn in a single user message, `tool_result` blocks first, each with its `tool_use_id`; split messages cause a 400.
Raw HTTP needs the key, `anthropic-version` and `content-type: application/json`; the official SDKs add them, retry transient errors twice and stream for you.
notes.tip: A stem about rebuilding, editing or truncating a conversation, or about lost tool context, is answered by the stateless design: the client resends full structured history, never flattened text.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[App stores history] --> B[Send system plus all messages]
  B --> C[Reply as content blocks]
  C --> D[Append reply and tool results]
  D --> B

notes.objective: Integrate Claude into CI/CD pipelines to analyze code submissions and provide structured feedback on pull requests using tool use and the Messages API.
notes.title: CI pipeline: headless Claude with a JSON schema
notes.gist: In CI, run Claude Code non-interactively with a JSON schema so findings arrive as validated data, not prose to scrape.
points: `claude -p` with a prompt runs non-interactively and exits 0 on success, non-zero on failure, so the job can branch on the status.
`--output-format json` returns the result plus session metadata; add `--json-schema` and the conforming object appears in `structured_output`, which is absent if Claude declined.
`--bare` skips hooks, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md so every runner behaves the same; it needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and is the recommended mode for scripts.
`--allowedTools` pre-approves only what the job needs, with prefix rules such as `Bash(git diff *)`; in a non-interactive run anything that would prompt is denied.
GitHub Action `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1`: key in `secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `claude_args` for `--max-turns`; a `prompt` input means automation mode, none means it waits for `@claude`.
notes.tip: When posting fails because output switches between tables, bullets and renamed fields, choose JSON output with a schema plus validation; regex parsing, stricter wording or a second Claude pass are the distractors.

flowchart LR

  B --> C{structured_output present and valid?}
  C -->|yes| D[Post inline comments]
  C -->|no| E[Fail the job or retry once]

notes.objective: Implement tool use patterns in code review systems to generate structured findings with specific fields such as file path, line number, severity, and remediation suggestions.
notes.title: Structured findings through tool use
notes.gist: Model each finding as a tool's input_schema so Claude returns typed fields, then use tool_choice and nullable fields to keep the output complete and honest.
points: A tool is `name` + detailed `description` + JSON `input_schema`; the reply is a `tool_use` block whose `input` is your object, such as findings with `file_path`, `line_number`, a `severity` enum and `remediation`.
`tool_choice`: `auto` (default, may answer in prose), `any` (must call one of the tools), `tool` (must call the named one), `none`; `any` and `tool` pre-fill the turn, so no prose precedes the call.
Use `any` when the tool is unknown at design time, such as routing a document to one of several extractors; force a named tool to run step one first, then call the next tool on the following turn.
Fields the source may not state (team, ticket id) should be nullable or optional with an instruction to return null; required fields push Claude to invent plausible values.
Current docs: Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 reject `any` and `tool` with a 400; use `auto` with `strict: true` or `output_config.format` there.
notes.tip: 'Sometimes returns an explanation instead of calling a tool' means tool_choice any; 'invented team names and ticket numbers' means nullable fields, not a sterner prompt; wrong tool order means force the first tool.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Finding schema as a tool] --> B{Must Claude call a tool every turn?}
  B -->|Yes, tool varies| C[tool_choice any]
  B -->|Yes, one specific tool| D[tool_choice tool with name]
  B -->|No| E[tool_choice auto]

notes.objective: Use the Message Batches API to process multiple code review tasks efficiently while handling custom tool calls for validation and analysis.
notes.title: Message Batches API: cost, limits, custom_id
notes.gist: Batches trade latency for half price, so use them for bulk work nobody waits on, and match results by custom_id, never by position.
points: 50 percent off input and output tokens; up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB per batch; most finish within 1 hour, and a batch expires after 24 hours.
Each request is a unique `custom_id` (1 to 64 characters) plus `params`; results arrive in any order as `.jsonl`, so join on `custom_id`; results stay downloadable for 29 days.
Result types are `succeeded`, `errored`, `canceled` and `expired`; only succeeded requests are billed and one failure never affects the rest; fix 400s, resubmit 5xx.
Tool use is allowed but nothing runs your client tool: a result can end in `tool_use`; run the tool yourself (for example a build validator) and submit a follow-up request with the `tool_result`.
A submitted batch cannot be edited: cancel it (status `canceling`, partial results kept) and resubmit; `params` are validated only after processing, so dry-run one request on the Messages API first.
notes.tip: 'Nightly', 'nobody waits' and 'tens of thousands of items' point to batches; 'a user waits for validation' or 'blocks the merge' point to the synchronous API.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Submit batch with custom_ids] --> B[Poll until processing_status is ended]
  B --> C[Stream results and join on custom_id]
  C --> D{Result ends in tool_use?}
  D -->|Yes| E[Run tool then submit follow-up batch]
  D -->|No| F[Store validated result]

notes.objective: Handle errors and unexpected outputs in extraction systems by implementing validation logic that ensures data quality before passing results to backend applications.
notes.title: Schema-valid is not the same as correct
notes.gist: Constrained decoding guarantees the shape of the JSON, so your code must still check meaning, stop_reason and failures before anything reaches a backend.
points: `output_config.format` (JSON outputs) and `strict: true` (tool inputs) use constrained decoding: the reply parses and has the required keys and types, with no retry needed for shape.
Shape is not meaning: a wrong total, a swapped date or an invented vendor still validates, so add business-rule and cross-field checks in your own code.
The guarantee can fail: `stop_reason: refusal` returns HTTP 200 with off-schema text, `max_tokens` truncates, and enum values may differ in capitalization; read `stop_reason` before parsing.
Supported subset: `additionalProperties: false`, no recursive schemas, no `minimum` or `maxLength`; the SDK `parse()` helper moves unsupported limits into descriptions and re-validates in code.
On a failed check, retry with the validator's error message fed back, a bounded number of times, then queue the record for human review; if the source never states the value, a retry cannot help.
notes.tip: 'Crashes one run in fifty on malformed JSON' wants schema enforcement, validation and retry with the error fed back; temperature 0, louder instructions and silently skipping bad records are the distractors.

flowchart TB
  A[Claude output] --> B{Schema and business rules ok?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Write to backend]
  B -->|No| D{Attempts left?}
  D -->|Yes| E[Retry with error fed back]
  D -->|No| F[Human review queue]
  E --> A

notes.objective: Design document processing pipelines that extract structured data from unstructured documents using Claude and validate outputs against JSON schemas.
notes.title: Feeding documents in: PDFs, images, Files API
notes.gist: Know the input blocks and the size limits so large documents are split or counted before they fail at upload.
points: PDFs go in `document` blocks as a URL, base64 (`application/pdf`) or a `file_id`; images use `image` blocks (jpeg, png, gif, webp); models take text and images, so audio needs transcribing first.
PDF limits: 32 MB per request and 600 pages (100 when the context window is under 1M tokens); dense pages can fill the context first, so split large files into sections.
A PDF page costs roughly 1,500 to 3,000 text tokens plus its page image; `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` returns an estimate before you send, for base64 PDFs only.

Files API: upload once (500 MB per file), reuse the `file_id`, delete when done; files you upload cannot be downloaded back, and `.docx` or `.xlsx` are not accepted in document blocks, so convert them to text or PDF before sending.
Place PDFs before the question text in the request; past the limits, chunk the corpus, summarise each chunk, then synthesise the summaries.
notes.tip: A stem saying users must never see an upload failure for 50 to 1,200 page files wants a size and token check before submission, plus chunking, not a larger max_tokens.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Incoming file] --> B{Within 32 MB and page limit?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Send document block or file_id]
  B -->|No| D[Split into sections]
  D --> C

notes.objective: Route documents to specialized extraction workflows based on content classification and integrate validated results with downstream business systems.
notes.title: Classify, route, then extract per type
notes.gist: A cheap classification step picks the specialised prompt and schema for each document type, and only validated output reaches backend systems.
points: Routing classifies the input, then hands it to a specialised follow-up with its own prompt, schema and tools; one shared prompt for every type lets tuning for one hurt the others.
Give the classifier one tool per workflow (`extract_invoice`, `extract_contract`) with `tool_choice` of `any`, so the reply is always a structured call, never an explanation; add an unknown route.
Send easy, high-volume classification to a small model such as Haiku and hard extraction to a larger one; routing only pays when classification is accurate.
Each branch has its own schema with nullable fields for absent values and its own validation rules; cross-field checks such as totals and dates run after extraction.
Hand backends only records that passed validation, with the document id and API `request-id` for tracing; low-confidence or unknown documents go to a human queue.
notes.tip: 'About 5 percent of calls return an explanation instead of a tool call' while the type is unknown at runtime means tool_choice any: auto still allows prose, a named tool hard-codes one schema, prefill is fragile.

flowchart TB
  A[Incoming document] --> B[Classify with tool_choice any]
  B --> C{Document type?}
  C -->|Invoice| D[Invoice prompt and schema]

notes.objective: Handle errors and unexpected outputs in extraction systems by implementing validation logic that ensures data quality before passing results to backend applications.
notes.title: stop_reason, retries and tool errors
notes.gist: Read stop_reason on every 200 response, retry only transient HTTP errors with backoff, and report tool failures inside the tool loop.
points: `stop_reason`: `end_turn` use it; `max_tokens` truncated, so raise the limit or continue; `tool_use` run the tool; `pause_turn` send the content back; `refusal` is a 200 with `stop_details`, not an error.
Retry only transient errors: 429 `rate_limit_error`, 500 `api_error`, 504 and 529 `overloaded_error`, with exponential backoff, jitter, the `retry-after` header and a retry cap.
Do not retry 400, 401, 403, 404 or 413: fix the request, key, permission or size (32 MB); a 429 without `retry-after` can be the monthly spend cap and keeps failing.
The SDKs already retry connection errors, 429 and 5xx twice with backoff (`max_retries`); a hand-written tight retry loop worsens an overload, and a queue absorbs bursts.
A tool failure goes back as a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and an instructive message in the same turn; a search with no matches is a successful empty result, not an error.
notes.tip: 'Truncated mid-sentence' means max_tokens; 'worked for months then 401' means an expired or rotated key; a retry storm calls for exponential backoff with jitter and a cap, never an immediate loop.

cards.q: Why must an app resend the whole conversation on every Messages API call?
cards.a: The API is stateless and keeps no history, so send every prior message, including tool_use and tool_result blocks, plus the system prompt, each time.

cards.q: Claude returns three tool_use blocks in one turn. How do you send the results back?
cards.a: In one user message: one tool_result per tool_use_id, all placed before any text. Separate messages per result cause a 400.

cards.q: In CI, which flags make `claude -p` return JSON that matches a schema, and where does the object appear?
cards.a: `--output-format json` with `--json-schema`; the object is in the `structured_output` field, which is missing if Claude declined, so check it first.

cards.q: Which tool_choice setting fixes a pipeline that sometimes gets prose instead of a tool call when the tool varies?
cards.a: Type `any`: Claude must call one of the provided tools. A named `tool` forces one specific tool; `auto` still allows prose.

cards.q: Code-review findings need a team and ticket id that the diff often lacks, and Claude invents them. What is the fix?
cards.a: Make those fields nullable or optional and tell Claude to return null when the source does not state them; required fields invite fabrication.

cards.q: What are the Message Batches API discount, size limits and timing?
cards.a: 50 percent off; 100,000 requests or 256 MB per batch; most finish within 1 hour, expiry at 24 hours; results kept 29 days.

cards.q: Batch results return in a different order than submitted. How do you match them to requests?
cards.a: By `custom_id`, 1 to 64 characters of letters, digits, hyphen or underscore. Result order is never guaranteed.

cards.q: A review task in a batch needs a client-side tool such as a build validator. How does it work?
cards.a: The batch only returns `tool_use`; you run the tool yourself and submit a follow-up request containing the `tool_result`.

cards.q: What does structured output guarantee, and what can still break the schema?
cards.a: Valid JSON in the schema's shape. A refusal or `max_tokens` cut-off can still break it, and a wrong value still validates.

cards.q: A schema-valid extraction has the wrong invoice total. What layer is missing, and what do you do on failure?
cards.a: Business-rule validation in your code. Retry with the validator's error fed back a bounded number of times, then send the record to human review.

cards.q: Which HTTP errors should a client retry with backoff, and which should it never retry?
cards.a: Retry 429, 500, 504 and 529 with exponential backoff, jitter and retry-after. Never retry 400, 401, 403 or 404; fix the request.

cards.q: A response ends with stop_reason max_tokens. What happened and what do you do?
cards.a: The output was cut off at your limit. Increase max_tokens or ask Claude to continue; a truncated tool_use block must be retried with a higher limit.

cards.q: A tool call times out. How do you tell Claude without losing the conversation context?
cards.a: Return a `tool_result` for that tool_use_id with `is_error: true` and an instructive message. A search with no matches is a normal empty result.

cards.q: What are the PDF limits for one Messages API request?
cards.a: 32 MB per request and 600 pages, or 100 pages when the context window is under 1M tokens. Use the Files API for large files.

cards.q: A classifier must route a document to one of four extraction tools, type unknown in advance. What routes reliably?
cards.a: Provide all four tools with tool_choice type `any`, so every reply is a tool call; add an unknown route for human review.

summary.tests: Whether you can match model tier, effort, processing mode and caching to a task's latency, accuracy and cost needs, pin versions safely and tell a model change from a configuration or data change.
must_know: Haiku is the lowest latency and price for classification, extraction, routing and subagents; Sonnet is the balanced everyday tier; Opus suits long agentic coding; Fable the hardest reasoning.
Decide by measuring on your own data: start efficiency-first or capability-first, and try lower effort before switching models.
Pin the exact model ID in production; aliases move, and a new release can change formatting, refusals or tool behavior, so migrate through your eval suite.
Batches are 50% off for work nobody waits on; streaming only improves perceived latency; a cache read costs a tenth of base input or less and a 5-minute write 1.25x.
Thinking tokens bill as output and count toward `max_tokens`; legacy `budget_tokens` is at least 1,024 and below `max_tokens`; newer models use adaptive thinking plus `effort`.
`max_tokens` is the only hard cap on a response; effort is a soft signal; temperature 0 is not determinism, and newer models reject sampling parameters.
Multi-agent systems use about 15x a chat's tokens, so they pay only for high-value, parallel, breadth-first work.
traps: Leaving an alias or 'latest' in production, so a new snapshot changes formatting or refusals overnight.
Picking the biggest model, or a batch job, because it sounds safer instead of measured accuracy, latency and who is waiting.
Setting a thinking budget above `max_tokens`, or sending a budget to a model that only has adaptive thinking, or expecting a lower `max_tokens` to cut the bill.

notes.objective: Select between Claude models based on task complexity, latency requirements, and cost constraints to optimize system performance.
notes.title: Pick the model tier by the task
notes.gist: Match the tier to the job, start from the cheapest or the strongest, and let your own evals decide.
points: Haiku 5.5 is the lowest latency and price (from $0.10 input and $0.50 output per million tokens) for classification, extraction, routing, real-time work and subagents.

Sonnet 5.5 ($2 and $10) is the speed-and-capability middle for everyday coding, analysis and tool use; Opus 5.5 ($4 and $20) for long agentic coding and refactors; Fable 5.1 ($10 and $50) for hours-long agents and the hardest reasoning.

Start efficiency-first (begin on Haiku, upgrade only for a capability gap) for prototypes, tight latency and high volume; start capability-first (begin on Opus, then trim) when accuracy outweighs cost.

Adjusting effort is frequently cheaper than changing models; to choose, build benchmark tests from your own prompts and data and compare accuracy, quality and edge cases, not vendor claims or what competitors picked.

Combine models: a small model does the bulk and escalates low-confidence cases, an orchestrator delegates bulk work to cheaper workers, and deterministic work such as unit conversion stays in plain code.
notes.tip: 'Millions of simple labels, tight latency, minimal cost' means the smallest tier after a benchmark check; 'planning drift across many interacting constraints' means the most capable tier; 'two teams disagree' means test on your own sample.

notes.objective: Select between Claude models based on task complexity, latency requirements, and cost constraints to optimize system performance.
notes.title: Prompt caching: pay once for the prefix
notes.gist: Cache the stable beginning of every request so repeated tokens are read at a fraction of the price and count less against rate limits.
points: The cached prefix is built in the order `tools`, `system`, `messages`: put static content first and anything variable (user turn, timestamp) last, with `cache_control` at the end of the static part; a change before the breakpoint invalidates it.
A cache read costs 0.1x the base input price (0.05x on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5); a 5-minute write costs 1.25x and a 1-hour write 2x, so one reuse already repays the 5-minute write.
The default lifetime is 5 minutes and is refreshed every time the prefix is used; add `ttl` of `1h` when requests are further apart; a prefix reused rarely only adds write fees.

Prompts below the minimum length are silently not cached (512 tokens on the newest models, 1,024 to 4,096 on older ones); if `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` are both 0, nothing was cached.
Cache reads do not count toward input-tokens-per-minute limits on most models, so caching also raises effective throughput; a request may carry up to 4 breakpoints.
notes.tip: The same 6,000-token policy text on every call with cost and latency climbing means static prefix first plus caching; 'cache never hits' means a prompt under the minimum, a changing prefix such as a timestamp, or gaps longer than the lifetime.

flowchart LR

  B --> C{Same prefix within lifetime?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Cache read at 0.1x]
  C -->|No| E[Cache write at 1.25x]

notes.objective: Evaluate and apply model versioning strategies (pinned versions, aliases, or latest) to balance stability, feature access, and change management requirements.
notes.title: Pin model IDs; migrate on purpose
notes.gist: A model ID is a frozen snapshot and an alias is a moving pointer, so production pins the ID and upgrades are evaluated releases.
points: Each model ID identifies a pinned version that stays constant for the life of that ID; updated weights ship under a new ID.

From the 4.6 generation the dateless ID (`claude-sonnet-4-6`, `claude-opus-5-5`) is itself the pinned snapshot; for earlier models the dated ID (`claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`) is pinned and the short alias (`claude-sonnet-4-5`) follows the newest dated snapshot.
Pin the exact ID in production and read it from per-environment configuration, not code, so test, staging and production cannot drift; keep aliases and brand-new models for experiments.
Lifecycle is active, legacy, deprecated, retired; Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice before retiring a public model, and the Console Usage export by API key and model finds calls still on it.

Migrate service by service: run your evaluation suite on the successor, compare, then switch traffic with checkpoints, because a new model can change formatting, instruction adherence or tool behavior.
notes.tip: 'Output structure changed overnight with no code change' plus an alias means pin the exact ID and migrate deliberately; 'pinned model retires in 75 days' means validate the successor against the eval suite, then a controlled release.

notes.objective: Implement asynchronous processing patterns (batching, streaming, or deferred execution) to meet throughput and cost requirements when latency constraints permit.
notes.title: Sync, streaming or batch: who is waiting?
notes.gist: Streaming improves perceived speed, batches cut cost for work nobody waits on, and neither replaces the other.
points: A user is waiting: synchronous call with `stream: true` so text appears as it is generated, using server-sent events over the same HTTP connection; streaming changes perceived latency, not total cost.

Nobody is waiting (nightly job, backlog, evals): Message Batches at 50% of the price with results inside 24 hours; a mixed system keeps the interactive path synchronous and sends the archive to batch.
Deferred execution when work outlasts a request: acknowledge at once and deliver the result by callback or polling; a queue absorbs bursts and keeps traffic inside rate limits without dropping work.
Many independent calls: use the SDK's async client with a concurrency cap sized to the RPM, ITPM and OTPM limits instead of a sequential loop.

Stream events run `message_start`, then per block `content_block_start`, `content_block_delta`, `content_block_stop` (grouped by `index`), `message_delta` (final `stop_reason`, cumulative usage), `message_stop`; tool input arrives as partial JSON in `input_json_delta`.
notes.tip: 'Results needed by morning' or '1.5 million invoices within 48 hours' means batches; 'first results in 500 ms' or 'users stare at a blank screen' means streaming, not a bigger model.

flowchart TB
  A{Who needs the answer?} -->|A user right now| B[Sync call with streaming]
  A -->|Nobody before a deadline| C[Message Batches]
  A -->|Caller moves on| D[Queue and callback]

notes.objective: Configure conditional feature usage (extended thinking, code execution, agentic loops) based on task characteristics to optimize latency and cost trade-offs.
notes.title: Effort and thinking: spend tokens where they pay
notes.gist: Thinking and effort add reasoning tokens, so raise them for tasks that benefit and cap them for the rest.
points: Reasoning tokens bill at the output rate and count toward `max_tokens` even when the thinking text is hidden; `max_tokens` is the hard ceiling, effort only a soft signal.

Newer models use adaptive thinking (Claude decides when and how much) steered by `output_config.effort` (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`); `thinking` of type `enabled` with `budget_tokens` returns a 400 on Claude 4.7 and later.
Legacy extended thinking (4.5 and earlier): `budget_tokens` is at least 1,024 and below `max_tokens`; start near 1,024 for simple tasks and at 16,000 or more for complex ones; above 32k use batches.

To cut cost or latency lower `effort` first (it also means fewer, terser tool calls); defaults differ (medium on Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, high elsewhere), and changing top-level effort mid-conversation invalidates the cache.
With tools, pass `thinking` blocks back unmodified, toggle thinking between turns not mid-turn, and remember manual extended thinking cannot be combined with forced `tool_choice` (`any` or `tool`).
notes.tip: 'Routine lookups take 5 to 10 seconds and burn tokens' means lower the effort or budget for those queries; 'a 400 after upgrading although the same request worked before' means the new model wants adaptive thinking plus effort, not a budget.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{Task needs deep reasoning?} -->|No| B[Low effort or no thinking]
  A -->|Yes| C[Adaptive thinking at high effort]
  C --> D[Set max_tokens as hard cap]
  B --> D

notes.objective: Design multi-agent system architectures that distribute specialized tasks across agents while managing coordination, context, and output quality.
notes.title: When multi-agent systems earn their cost
notes.gist: Extra agents buy parallelism and capacity at roughly 15 times the tokens of a chat, so reserve them for valuable, breadth-first work.
points: Orchestrator-worker: a lead agent plans, spawns subagents that search at the same time, each in its own context window, then synthesises; an Opus lead with Sonnet subagents beat single-agent Opus by 90.2% on Anthropic's research eval.
Cost: agents use about 4x the tokens of a chat and multi-agent systems about 15x, so the task's value must pay for it; token usage alone explained 80% of the variance on BrowseComp.
Poor fit: work where agents must share one context or depend heavily on each other, such as most coding tasks; good fit: heavy parallelization, information beyond one window, many complex tools.
Scale effort to the query: 1 agent and 3 to 10 tool calls for a fact, 2 to 4 subagents with 10 to 15 calls each for a comparison, more than 10 subagents for complex research.

Manage context and quality: brief each subagent with objective, output format, tool guidance and boundaries, save the plan to memory before the window fills, and let subagents store artifacts and return references.
notes.tip: A stem asking whether to split a tightly coupled coding task across agents wants no, because coordination cost beats the parallel gain; a wide, independent research sweep wants parallel subagents.

flowchart TB
  A[Lead agent plans and saves plan] --> B[Spawn 3 to 5 subagents in parallel]
  B --> C[Subagents search in own contexts]
  C --> D{Enough coverage?}
  D -->|No| B
  D -->|Yes| E[Lead writes final answer]

notes.objective: Diagnose model behavior changes and performance degradation by distinguishing between model updates, configuration drift, and prompt/data variations.
notes.title: Diagnosing a behavior change
notes.gist: Separate the suspects (model, serving layer, configuration, prompt or data) by changing one at a time against a fixed eval set.
points: Check the model string first: an alias or unpinned ID can move to a new snapshot; a pinned ID keeps its weights, but the router, safety classifiers and sampling logic around it can change and shift behavior slightly.

Diff the request configuration: model, system prompt, tools, `tool_choice`, `max_tokens`, effort and thinking; defaults differ per model, and newer ones reject `temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k` (400), prefill and `thinking` of type `enabled`.
Claude 4.7 and later use a tokenizer that yields roughly 30% extra tokens on identical input, so cost and limits shift with no prompt change; count tokens with the target model's ID.
Check prompt and data drift: longer or different inputs, context growing each turn, retrieval returning other chunks; quality falls as irrelevant context piles up.
Reproduce with a fixed evaluation set run on old and new versions; temperature 0 does not guarantee identical output, so judge by pass rates, not a single diff.
notes.tip: 'Accuracy dropped, nobody changed code, prompt or config' with an alias in use points to a model update; 'the same request now returns 400' points to a removed parameter; identical input giving different text is normal variance.

notes.objective: Match document processing workflows to appropriate Claude capabilities (extraction, structured output, batch processing) based on latency, accuracy, and volume requirements.
notes.title: Match the document workflow to the feature
notes.gist: Choose the capability by the constraint that binds: structure, volume, latency, repeated context or accuracy.
points: Typed fields for a database: structured outputs (`output_config.format` or strict tools) so the shape is guaranteed, plus validation for meaning.
High volume with no waiting user: Message Batches at 50% off; the same document queried many times: cache the document, and the cache discount stacks with the batch discount.
Interactive intake forms: a synchronous call on a fast tier such as Haiku, streamed if text is shown, with larger models reserved for cases that fail validation.
PDFs and scans go in `document` blocks that give Claude text and page images, so charts and tables are read; put the PDF before the question and split very long files.
Citations ground answers in the source but cannot be combined with `output_config.format`; context beyond the window means chunk and summarise, or retrieve only the relevant sections.
notes.tip: Pick the feature that removes the stated constraint: 'must finish while staff wait' is sync, 'backlog of 35,000 documents' is batch, 'inconsistent field names' is a schema or examples, 'same manual asked repeatedly' is caching.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Document workload] --> B{Binding constraint?}
  B -->|Typed fields| C[Structured output and validation]
  B -->|Volume, nobody waiting| D[Batch plus caching]
  B -->|Live user| E[Sync on a small tier with streaming]

cards.q: Which Claude tier fits a high-volume classification or routing workload with tight latency and cost limits?
cards.a: Haiku, the fastest and cheapest tier, after confirming accuracy on a benchmark of your own data; escalate only hard or low-confidence cases.

cards.q: Two teams disagree on Haiku versus Sonnet for document analysis, citing industry reports and benchmarks. How do you decide?
cards.a: Test both on a representative sample of your own documents against your quality bar, then weigh accuracy against cost and latency.

cards.q: What is the difference between a pinned model ID and an alias, and which belongs in production?
cards.a: A pinned ID is a fixed snapshot; an alias moves to the newest snapshot. Pin the exact ID in production and migrate through your eval suite.

cards.q: A pipeline that references an alias started returning a different JSON structure overnight. What fixes it?
cards.a: Pin the exact model ID, read from per-environment config, and move to new versions only after the evaluation suite passes.

cards.q: How much notice does Anthropic give before retiring a public model, and how do you find your usage?
cards.a: At least 60 days. Export usage by API key and model from the Console Usage page to find calls still on the old model.

cards.q: Which workloads belong in the Batches API and which stay synchronous?
cards.a: Batches for non-urgent bulk work, such as nightly or backlog jobs, at 50% off. Anything with a user waiting stays synchronous, usually streamed.

cards.q: Users stare at a blank screen for several seconds before the full answer appears. What is the fix?
cards.a: Stream the response so tokens display as they are generated. It improves perceived latency, not total cost.

cards.q: What does prompt caching cost compared with normal input tokens?
cards.a: A cache read costs 0.1x the base input price (0.05x on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5); a 5-minute write costs 1.25x, a 1-hour write 2x.

cards.q: A cache_control marker on a 650-token system prompt never produces cache hits or writes. Why?
cards.a: The prompt is below the minimum cacheable length and is silently skipped; the newest models need 512 tokens, older ones 1,024 to 4,096.

cards.q: Cache writes happen on almost every request but cache reads are rare. What are the likely causes?
cards.a: The prefix changes (timestamps, reordered blocks), requests arrive further apart than the 5-minute lifetime, or the breakpoint sits on varying content.

cards.q: How are thinking tokens billed, and what limit must exceed the legacy thinking budget?
cards.a: They bill as output tokens and count toward max_tokens. `budget_tokens` must be at least 1,024 and below max_tokens.

cards.q: Sending `thinking` of type enabled with `budget_tokens` to a Claude 4.7 or later model returns a 400. What replaces it?
cards.a: Adaptive thinking, steered by `output_config.effort` (low, medium, high, xhigh, max). Lower effort first to cut cost or latency.

cards.q: Do `max_tokens` and effort cap spending in the same way?
cards.a: No. `max_tokens` is the hard ceiling on output, and billing counts tokens actually generated. Effort is only a soft signal.

cards.q: How many times a chat's tokens does a multi-agent research system use, and when is it worth it?
cards.a: About 15x (a single agent about 4x). Worth it for high-value, parallel, breadth-first work; poor for tightly coupled tasks such as most coding.

cards.q: Costs and token counts rose after moving to Claude 4.7 or later with no prompt change. Why?
cards.a: A newer tokenizer yields roughly 30% extra tokens on identical input. Re-count tokens with the target model's ID before forecasting.

summary.tests: Whether you can choose between a fixed workflow and an agent, and build a coordinator with scoped subagents that get explicit context, run in parallel, return structured findings and are gated by deterministic checks.
must_know: Workflows follow predefined code paths; agents let the model direct its own steps. Known, fixed steps mean a deterministic workflow; unpredictable steps mean an agent with a stop condition.
The agent loop repeats while `stop_reason` is `tool_use`: run every tool, return all results in one user message, finish on `end_turn`; cap it with `max_turns` and `max_budget_usd`.
A subagent starts with fresh context: only the Agent tool's prompt string reaches it, so put findings, IDs and constraints in it; only its final message comes back.
The coordinator needs `Agent` (formerly `Task`) in `allowedTools`; give each subagent only the `tools` its role needs.
Independent subtasks go out in one turn and run in parallel; dependent ones wait; the coordinator reconciles results and keeps source attribution.
Enforce ordering and approvals in code (hooks, prerequisite gates), not in prompts; route every handoff through the coordinator.
Resume continues a session, fork branches it, and a fresh session with a summary beats resuming stale context; MCP tools are named `mcp__server__tool`.
traps: Assuming a subagent sees the coordinator's history or an earlier subagent's findings instead of passing them in its prompt.
Letting workers message each other or spawn their own workers, which removes coordinator visibility, instead of routing through the coordinator.
Relying on a system-prompt instruction for a must-happen step (audit, approval, ordering) instead of a hook or gate.

notes.objective: Design a multi-agent system architecture where a coordinator agent delegates specialized tasks to subagents and orchestrates their contributions toward a unified goal.
notes.title: Workflow or agent: who controls the path?
notes.gist: Use fixed code for known steps and an agent only when the path depends on what it finds.
points: Workflows run LLMs and tools along predefined code paths; agents let the LLM direct its own process and tool use; start with the simplest design and add complexity only when it measurably helps.

Five patterns: prompt chaining (fixed subtasks with gates), routing (classify, then specialize), parallelization (sectioning or voting), orchestrator-workers (subtasks decided at run time), evaluator-optimizer (generate, critique, loop).
Fixed, known steps in a fixed order with checkable output, such as parse, validate, report, belong in a deterministic workflow: cheaper, testable and auditable.
Choose an agent when steps cannot be known until intermediate results are seen (open-ended research, multi-file coding); give it an explicit success condition, a step ceiling and sandboxed testing.
Agents trade latency and cost for flexibility and can compound errors; frameworks can hide the prompts, so start with direct API calls.
notes.tip: 'The same five steps for every input' means a deterministic workflow, not an autonomous agent; 'the number of subtasks depends on the input' means orchestrator-workers; 'different ticket types need different prompts' means routing.

flowchart TB

  A -->|No| C[Agent or orchestrator-workers]

notes.objective: Design a multi-agent system architecture where a coordinator agent delegates specialized tasks to subagents and orchestrates their contributions toward a unified goal.
notes.title: The agent loop: tool_use until end_turn
notes.gist: An agent is a loop that runs the tools Claude requests and feeds results back until Claude stops asking for tools.
points: Raw Messages API loop: call, and while `stop_reason` is `tool_use` execute every `tool_use` block, append the assistant turn and one user message holding all `tool_result` blocks, then call again; stop on `end_turn`.
Stop conditions belong in code: end when a response has no `tool_use` blocks, with a ceiling (`max_turns`, `max_budget_usd`) as a backstop; an agent that keeps calling tools usually lacks that check.
The Agent SDK runs this loop for you, with built-in tools, permissions, automatic compaction and sessions; the Client SDK leaves the loop to you or to its beta tool runner.
`ResultMessage.subtype` says how it ended: `success`, `error_max_turns`, `error_max_budget_usd` or `error_during_execution`; the `result` text exists only on success.
Read-only tools may run concurrently while state-changing ones (Edit, Write, Bash) run in sequence; `max_turns` counts tool-use turns only, and the budget cap includes subagent spend.
notes.tip: 'The agent keeps calling tools after the answer' means the loop never checks for a response without `tool_use`; 'the bill exploded on a vague prompt' means set `max_turns` and `max_budget_usd` and inspect the result subtype.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Send messages and tools] --> B{stop_reason is tool_use?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Run every tool call]
  C --> D[Append results in one user message]
  D --> A
  B -->|No| E[Return the final answer]

notes.objective: Configure specialized subagents to perform domain-specific analysis tasks such as document review, data auditing, research synthesis, or code examination.
notes.title: Define scoped subagents with AgentDefinition
notes.gist: A subagent is a separate agent with its own prompt, tools and model, invoked through the Agent tool and isolated from the parent's context.
points: `AgentDefinition` needs a `description` (when Claude should delegate) and a `prompt` (its system prompt); optional fields include `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `skills`, `mcpServers`, `maxTurns`, `effort` and `permissionMode`.

Claude delegates through the `Agent` tool (called `Task` in older versions), so `Agent` must be in the coordinator's `allowedTools` or no subagent runs; naming the subagent in the prompt forces its use.
Least privilege: list only the `tools` a role needs, such as `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob` for a reviewer; if you omit the field the subagent inherits every tool, and a tool left out is simply absent.

Context isolation: the subagent works in its own window, intermediate tool calls stay inside, and only its final message returns, so exploring dozens of files adds a summary, not a transcript, to the parent.

Match model and effort to the role (a small model or low effort for lookups, a stronger one for high-stakes review); Claude Code also ships read-only `Explore` and `Plan` helpers for search and planning.
notes.tip: 'Delegation is announced but no subagent runs' means `Agent` is missing from `allowedTools`; 'the subagent edited files it should only read' means its `tools` list was omitted or too broad.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Coordinator with Agent in allowedTools] --> B[Agent tool call with a prompt string]
  B --> C[Subagent with own prompt and tools]
  C --> D[Final message returns to coordinator]

notes.objective: Implement agent-to-agent communication patterns that enable subagents to receive delegated tasks from a coordinator and return findings for synthesis.
notes.title: Handoffs: pass context in, get findings out
notes.gist: Subagents see only what the coordinator writes into the delegation prompt, so every handoff must carry the facts, constraints and output format.
points: A non-fork subagent receives its own system prompt, the Agent tool's prompt string and project CLAUDE.md, but never the parent's history, tool results or system prompt.
A good brief states the objective, upstream findings with source metadata, IDs and file paths, constraints, success criteria and the output format; vague briefs make subagents duplicate or miss work.
Sequential dependencies: the coordinator accumulates earlier findings and threads them into the next subagent's prompt; a later agent without them contradicts the earlier ones.
Return structured findings (claim, source, date, evidence, confidence) instead of prose or whole transcripts; large artifacts go to files or storage with a lightweight reference passed back.
Route every handoff through the coordinator so it keeps visibility, control and logging; peer-to-peer messages between workers bypass it.
notes.tip: 'The third subagent contradicts the first two' means the findings were not passed into its prompt; 'quality dropped after adding a subagent' means the handoff lost context the main agent held.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Coordinator gathers facts] --> B[Prompt with context and format]
  B --> C[Subagent works in fresh context]
  C --> D[Structured findings returned]
  D --> A

notes.objective: Develop coordination logic that aggregates, synthesizes, or processes outputs from multiple subagents to produce final results or recommendations.
notes.title: Fan out in parallel, then synthesize
notes.gist: Split independent work across subagents in one turn, then reconcile the structured results while keeping provenance and conflicts visible.
points: Decompose into independent streams (sector, jurisdiction, document) and issue all subagent calls in one turn so they run concurrently; in Anthropic's research system 3 to 5 parallel subagents plus parallel tool calls cut time by up to 90%.
Dependent steps stay sequential: run a discovery phase first, then let the coordinator build follow-up subtasks from what it found instead of a fixed script.
Synthesize only structured outputs, keep each claim's source, date and method, and annotate conflicting values with both sources instead of silently picking one.

Validate before finishing: the coordinator checks the draft against the original request, finds unaddressed parts and sends targeted follow-ups; per-document passes then a cross-document reconciliation pass beat one giant pass.
`SubagentStart` and `SubagentStop` hooks fire as workers spawn and finish, which is where you track and collect parallel results.
notes.tip: 'Slow because the subagents run one after another' means issue the independent calls in one coordinator turn; 'two sources give conflicting statistics' means preserve both with attribution and flag the conflict.

notes.objective: Build multi-tier agent hierarchies where a primary coordinator validates inputs, distributes work to specialized subagents, and manages task dependencies.
notes.title: Hierarchies: validate, gate, order
notes.gist: The primary coordinator validates input, activates only the relevant specialists and enforces order and approvals in code.
points: The top tier validates and triages: verify identity and inputs first, classify the request, then activate only the relevant specialist workers, each with a focused scope.

Enforce prerequisites programmatically: a gate or `PreToolUse` hook blocks `process_refund` until the customer and order lookups return matching, eligible results; prompt instructions fail some of the time.
Risky tools such as `submit_refund_request` or `route_to_specialist` stay coordinator-controlled, while a read-only lookup can be delegated to a specialist.
Hooks give deterministic control: `PreToolUse` returns `allow`, `deny`, `ask` or `defer` (deny wins), `PostToolUse` can replace output with `updatedToolOutput`, `SubagentStop` collects results.

Subagents can spawn their own (default depth 3, set by `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH`), up to 20 run at once and `max_budget_usd` caps the whole tree; keep trees shallow so the coordinator keeps visibility.
notes.tip: 'Skips the audit about 5 percent of the time' or 'sometimes calls payment before verification' means a deterministic hook or gate, not a stronger prompt; 'unwanted deep chains of agents' means cap the depth.

notes.title: Connect agents to MCP servers
notes.gist: Register servers by transport, allow their tools by name, and keep credentials in the environment.
points: Pick the transport from the server's docs: a command to run means stdio, a URL means HTTP or SSE (with `headers` for auth), and your own in-process tools mean an SDK MCP server.

Register servers in code (`mcpServers`) or in a project-root `.mcp.json` that the team shares through version control, with `${ENV_VAR}` expansion for secrets; personal or experimental servers stay in user or local scope.

MCP tools are named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`; allow them in `allowedTools` with a wildcard such as `mcp__github__*` or one exact name, and check the init message for `connected`, `failed` or `needs-auth`.
Tool descriptions drive selection: state purpose, inputs, outputs, limits and how the tool differs from similar ones; a read-only database server config limits the damage of a wrong query.
Many MCP tools bloat context, so tool search defers their schemas by default; static catalogs fit MCP resources, while actions that change state stay tools.
notes.tip: 'The shared server config must live in the repo without secrets' means `.mcp.json` with environment-variable references; 'the agent cannot reach the backend' means check the server status in the init message first.

notes.title: Sessions and state: resume, fork, restart
notes.gist: Resume to continue, fork to branch, and start fresh with a summary when the old context is stale.
points: `continue` reopens whichever session in the working directory is newest and `resume` takes a session ID; both restore the full history, and `resume` is needed when several sessions exist, such as one per user.

`fork_session` copies the history into a new session with its own ID and leaves the original unchanged, so you can compare two approaches from one baseline; it branches the conversation, not the files.
When earlier findings are stale (changed policies or sources), start a fresh session seeded with a structured summary of what is still valid and a flag for what to re-check, rather than resuming.
A session is a file on the machine that ran it; for CI or serverless attach a session store, or pass the results you need as application state into a new session's prompt.
Long-running agents persist plans and decisions to files or a database so they survive compaction and restarts, and make steps idempotent so work resumes from a known point.
notes.tip: 'Test two competing approaches without losing the baseline' means fork; 'the agent restarts from scratch after an infrastructure restart' means external checkpoints and idempotent steps.

cards.q: What separates a workflow from an agent?
cards.a: In a workflow the control flow is fixed in code in advance; in an agent the model chooses its next step and tools.

cards.q: When is a deterministic workflow better than an autonomous agent?
cards.a: When the steps and their order are known and each output is checkable: it is cheaper, testable and auditable. Use an agent when steps depend on intermediate results.

cards.q: Name the five workflow patterns in Anthropic's Building effective agents.
cards.a: Prompt chaining, routing, parallelization (sectioning or voting), orchestrator-workers, and evaluator-optimizer.

cards.q: In a hand-written agent loop, when does it continue and when does it stop?
cards.a: Continue while stop_reason is tool_use: run all tools, return results in one user message. Stop on end_turn, with a turn or budget ceiling as backstop.

cards.q: Which two SDK options cap a runaway agent, and how do you see which one fired?
cards.a: `max_turns` and `max_budget_usd`. The ResultMessage subtype is error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd; the result text exists only on success.

cards.q: A coordinator announces delegation but no subagent ever runs. What is missing?
cards.a: The `Agent` tool (formerly `Task`) is not in the coordinator's `allowedTools`, so Claude cannot invoke any subagent.

cards.q: What does a subagent receive from its parent, and what does it not?
cards.a: Its own prompt, the Agent tool's prompt string and project CLAUDE.md. Not the parent's conversation history, tool results or system prompt.

cards.q: A third subagent contradicts the findings of the first two. What is the fix?
cards.a: The coordinator accumulates the earlier findings and includes them explicitly in the third subagent's prompt; findings do not propagate automatically.

cards.q: What four things belong in every delegation brief to a subagent?
cards.a: Its goal, the format of the answer, which tools and sources to use, and where the task stops.

cards.q: How do you run independent subtasks concurrently with subagents?
cards.a: Have the coordinator issue all the independent Agent calls in one turn, then collect and reconcile; wall time is the slowest subagent, not the sum.

cards.q: How should a synthesis step treat conflicting values from two subagents?
cards.a: Keep both with their sources, dates and methods and flag the conflict; never silently choose one or drop attribution.

cards.q: An agent sometimes skips a required audit or approval despite prompt instructions. What is the reliable fix?
cards.a: A deterministic gate or hook, such as PreToolUse, that blocks the action until the prerequisite passes. Prompts only influence the model.

cards.q: When several PreToolUse hooks disagree, which decision wins?
cards.a: Deny takes priority over defer, then ask, then allow.

cards.q: How does `resume` differ from `fork_session` in the Agent SDK?
cards.a: Resume continues the same session; fork copies its history into a new session with its own ID and leaves the original unchanged. Files are not branched.

cards.q: How do MCP tools appear to an SDK agent, and how do you allow every tool of one server?
cards.a: As `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. Allow a whole server with a wildcard such as `mcp__github__*` in `allowedTools`.

summary.tests: Whether you can write prompts and manage context so extraction, code review and multi-step agent work stay accurate: standing rules in the system prompt, examples, measurable criteria, document-first ordering and lean, curated context.
must_know: Stable role and rules go in the `system` prompt and per-request data in the user turn; repeating guidelines in every user message wastes tokens and drifts.
Two to five diverse examples in `<example>` tags fix inconsistent format and edge cases better than more rules; an instruction that contradicts an example gives unpredictable output.
Replace vague words (concise, professional, be conservative) with measurable criteria: categories, severity levels, thresholds and code examples.
Put long documents first and the question last (up to 30% better), separate parts with XML tags, and ask for quotes before analysis.
Input, output, tools and thinking all count toward the window (1M tokens on current models); accuracy falls as irrelevant tokens pile up, so retrieve only what the question needs.
Long sessions: compaction, tool-result clearing (default trigger 100,000 input tokens), notes outside the window, subagents that return 1,000 to 2,000 token summaries.
CLAUDE.md is advisory context kept under about 200 lines; path-scoped `.claude/rules/` and skills load on demand; a hook is what guarantees an action.
traps: Fixing inconsistent output by adding more rules or capital letters instead of two to four concrete examples.
Stuffing everything into the prompt in case it helps, instead of retrieving only the sections the question needs.
Asking a review prompt to be 'conservative' or 'high-confidence' instead of listing exactly what is reportable.

notes.objective: Design prompts that extract structured data from unstructured documents and validate outputs against formal schemas.
notes.title: Extraction prompts: examples, nulls, enums
notes.gist: Show the exact output you want, let the schema admit missing data, and give categories an honest escape hatch.
points: Give 2 to 4 diverse input and ideal-output pairs (the docs suggest 3 to 5) wrapped in `<example>` tags, covering awkward layouts such as footnotes, tables and inline citations; examples beat prose rules for format consistency.
Define the output as a tool `input_schema` or `output_config.format`; mark fields the document may not contain as nullable and say to return null instead of guessing.

Closed enums need an escape hatch: add `other` or `unclear` plus a free-text detail field (payment type `other` with a `payment_detail` string) so odd values are captured, not forced into a wrong label.

Prefilling an opening brace to force JSON works only on older models; Claude 4.6 and later return a 400, so use structured outputs, a tool schema or a system instruction; strip stray markdown fences before parsing if they appear.
Wrap each source document in tags with a `source` field, put documents above the instructions, and ask for quoted evidence per extracted field to cut guessing on long inputs.
notes.tip: Inconsistent field names or formats point to examples and a schema; invented values point to nullable fields; 'a new document type does not fit the categories' points to an enum escape hatch. Re-prompting harder is rarely the answer.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Source document in tags] --> B[Prompt with 2 to 4 examples]
  B --> C[Schema with nullable fields]
  C --> D[Claude output]
  D --> E[Validate against the schema]

notes.objective: Build extraction pipelines that consolidate information from multiple source documents into unified, validated structured outputs.
notes.title: Consolidating many documents into one record
notes.gist: Extract per document or section first, then reconcile in a separate pass that keeps every fact's source.
points: Process each document or section in its own focused pass with structured output, then run a dedicated cross-document reconciliation pass; one giant pass loses details in the middle.
Tag every extracted fact with source document id, section and a supporting excerpt, and carry that evidence through synthesis so each final row stays traceable.
Reconciliation merges duplicates, normalizes entity names, checks schema compliance and flags conflicting values with both sources instead of choosing one.

Independent categories in one large document can be extracted in parallel with shared document context, then merged and validated; dependent steps are chained with a programmatic gate between them (prompt chaining).
Have a fresh Claude session review the result: it receives only the source, the extracted fields and a rubric, not the extraction reasoning, so it is not biased toward its own output.
notes.tip: 'Stakeholders cannot trace a row back to its source' means carry excerpts and locations through the pipeline; 'values from different documents disagree' means annotate the conflict; 'quality drops on long multi-section packets' means per-section passes plus reconciliation.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Documents or sections] --> B[Per-item extraction with sources]
  B --> C[Reconciliation pass]
  C --> D{Conflicts or gaps?}
  D -->|Yes| E[Flag with both sources]
  D -->|No| F[Validated unified record]

notes.objective: Construct system prompts and context windows that balance comprehensive instruction coverage with token efficiency and clarity.
notes.title: System prompt versus user message
notes.gist: Standing role and rules belong in the system prompt, variable data in the user turn, and every instruction should be clear and measurable.
points: Put role, tone and standing constraints in `system` (applies to every turn, outside user control, no repeated tokens); per-request data and the question go in `messages`. claude.ai wraps a chat in its own system prompt and features; through the API you supply the system prompt yourself, so copy over any instructions you rely on.
Be clear and direct: state the output format and constraints, replace vague words (professional, concise) with measurable limits such as sentence counts, and apply the colleague test.
Say what to do, not only what not to do, and give the reason (the text is read aloud, so avoid ellipses); positive wording plus a sample beats a list of prohibitions.
Use XML tags to separate instructions, context, examples and inputs, with consistent tag names; one sentence of role in the system prompt focuses tone and expertise.
Keep instructions consistent: a rule that contradicts an example gives unpredictable behavior; aim for the right altitude, specific enough to guide without brittle if-else logic.
notes.tip: Guidelines pasted into every user message that drift over long conversations belong in the system prompt; 'drafts vary wildly in length' wants measurable limits; 'follows the examples but ignores a rule' hints at a contradiction.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[System prompt: role, rules, format] --> C[Claude]
  B[User turn: data and question] --> C
  C --> D[Output]

notes.objective: Craft prompts for code review systems that deliver specific, actionable feedback on code quality, security, and test coverage.
notes.title: Code review prompts that get acted on
notes.gist: Developers ignore vague or noisy reviews, so define what is reportable, show examples and keep the output structured.
points: Replace abstract language such as 'be conservative' or 'only high-confidence findings' with explicit categories, severity levels and a concrete code example of each finding type.

Define reportable criteria per area: performance (unbounded input processing, hot paths, repeated database calls in loops), security (injection, authentication, secrets), tests (changed branches without coverage).

Cut false positives by saying what to skip (style preferences, unchanged code) and to report only findings that change correctness or break a stated requirement; a reviewer asked to find problems will otherwise invent some.
Different file types need different rules: path-scoped files in `.claude/rules/` (migrations, generated clients, frontend) load only for matching paths, instead of one global review prompt.

Review in a fresh session or subagent that is shown just the diff and the criteria (Writer/Reviewer), return findings as schema-conforming JSON, and on re-runs pass prior findings so only new or unresolved issues are reported.
notes.tip: 'Developers ignore most comments' or 'too many false positives' means explicit reportable criteria with examples, not a stricter confidence threshold; 'the same review for every file type' means path-scoped rules.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Diff plus review criteria] --> B[Fresh reviewer context]
  B --> C[Findings as JSON with severity]
  C --> D{Matches reportable criteria?}
  D -->|Yes| E[Post inline comment]
  D -->|No| F[Drop as noise]

notes.objective: Construct system prompts and context windows that balance comprehensive instruction coverage with token efficiency and clarity.
notes.title: Context window: budget, rot and counting
notes.gist: The whole request, output included, uses up the window, and more context is not better context.
points: The window holds the system prompt, every message with its tool results, images and documents, the tool definitions and the reply including thinking; current models have 1M tokens and up to 128k output tokens.

Input alone over the window returns a 400 'prompt is too long'; on Claude 4.5 and later, input plus `max_tokens` over the window is accepted and may end with `model_context_window_exceeded`, while older models return a validation error.
Context rot: as tokens grow, accuracy and recall fall, so curate; retrieve only the relevant sections (the top few excerpts, not 100) instead of pasting a whole catalog or knowledge base.
Count before sending with the token counting endpoint (an estimate); tokenizers differ by model and language, and images and PDF pages add tokens.
Order matters in long prompts: documents first, question last (up to 30% better), important instructions at the edges rather than buried mid-prompt; a stable prefix first also enables caching.
notes.tip: 'Request rejected although the document fits' hints that input and `max_tokens` share the window on older models; 'answers got worse after adding more documents' means context rot, so retrieve less; 'upload failure for long documents' means count tokens first.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[System, tools, messages] --> B[Count tokens before sending]
  B --> C{Fits window with max_tokens?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Send the request]
  C -->|No| E[Trim, retrieve or chunk]

notes.objective: Construct system prompts and context windows that balance comprehensive instruction coverage with token efficiency and clarity.
notes.title: Keeping long sessions lean
notes.gist: Prune, summarize or offload context before it rots: compaction, tool-result clearing, notes and subagents.
points: Compaction summarizes a conversation near its limit and restarts with the summary (server-side compaction is in beta, Claude Code compacts automatically); aggressive compaction can lose subtle details, so tune what to keep.

Tool result clearing (`clear_tool_uses_20250919`) drops old tool results past a trigger (default 100,000 input tokens) and keeps the last 3 tool uses; `clear_at_least` and `exclude_tools` tune it, and clearing invalidates cached prefixes.
Structured notes (NOTES.md, a task list, a progress log) written outside the window survive resets and let the agent resume; a persistent fact store beats relying on a compressed history.
Subagents absorb noisy exploration in their own windows and return a distilled summary (often 1,000 to 2,000 tokens); tools should return only high-signal fields, not 50,000-token payloads.
Unrelated tasks get a new session (`/clear` in Claude Code) so earlier cases do not leak into later answers; retrieval tools load documents just in time instead of up front.
notes.tip: 'Slowly degrading, repeating itself, window full of verbose tool output' means prune and summarize tool output, compact history and isolate subtasks; 'resets lose the plan' means notes outside the window.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Context near its limit] --> B{What is filling it?}
  B -->|Old tool results| C[Clear tool results]
  B -->|Long history| D[Compact into a summary]
  B -->|Noisy exploration| E[Move it to a subagent]

notes.objective: Construct system prompts and context windows that balance comprehensive instruction coverage with token efficiency and clarity.
notes.title: Standing instructions: CLAUDE.md, rules, skills
notes.gist: Advisory files that load every session should be short; load specialist guidance only when it applies.
points: CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration: Claude usually follows it, but only a hook guarantees an action; keep each file under about 200 lines and cut anything Claude can infer from the code.

Scopes: managed policy (organization), user (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`), project (`./CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, shared in git) and `CLAUDE.local.md` (personal, gitignored); `/init` drafts one and `/context` shows which memory files loaded.
`@path` imports tidy a long file but save no tokens, since the imported text loads at launch too.
`.claude/rules/*.md` files with `paths` globs in YAML frontmatter load only when Claude touches matching files, which suits migrations, tests or frontend code; rules without `paths` load at launch.
Skills (`SKILL.md` plus supporting files) load on demand through progressive disclosure, so reference workflows and house style cost tokens only when used.
notes.tip: 'A 1,500-line root file and instructions ignored' means split into path-scoped rules or skills and keep the root short; 'a guideline must never be skipped' means a hook, not CLAUDE.md.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{Instruction scope?} -->|Every session| B[Short CLAUDE.md]
  A -->|Only some file paths| C[Rule file with paths glob]
  A -->|Occasional workflow| D[Skill loaded on demand]
  A -->|Must always happen| E[Hook]

notes.objective: Implement multi-turn agent workflows that coordinate specialized subagents to handle complex, multi-part user requests.
notes.title: Prompts for multi-part requests
notes.gist: A coordinator prompt decomposes the request, gives each worker one concern with shared facts, then checks the draft against every part.
points: Decompose a request with several issues (a return, a duplicate charge, an address change) into one concern per subagent, and pass pre-verified shared facts such as customer identity and transaction records in each prompt.
Frame delegations around the goal: objective, context, constraints, success criteria and required output format, leaving the worker free to choose its approach instead of a rigid step script.
Route only to relevant specialists: classify intent and complexity first, then synthesize their findings into one response.
After synthesis the coordinator validates the draft against the original message, finds unaddressed concerns and sends targeted follow-up work before replying.
Interdependent checks run as a sequential chain (each item alone, then a final reconciliation); independent items run in parallel.
notes.tip: 'The reply ignores one of the customer's issues' means the coordinator should validate the draft against the original request and follow up; 'subagents duplicate each other' means non-overlapping scopes and shared facts in each prompt.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Multi-part request] --> B[Decompose by concern]
  B --> C[Specialists get shared facts]
  C --> D{Draft covers every part?}
  D -->|No| E[Targeted follow-up work]
  D -->|Yes| F[Send one unified reply]

summary.tests: Whether you can connect and secure MCP servers, design tool sets that agents choose between correctly, and make tools fail in ways the agent can recover from.
must_know: An MCP server exposes tools (actions the model calls), resources (data you reference) and prompts (user-run templates), and one server serves every MCP client.
stdio is a local subprocess that speaks over stdout, so log to stderr; shared remote servers use Streamable HTTP, SSE is deprecated, and the Messages API connector reaches only public HTTPS servers.
Project scope stores `.mcp.json` in the repo with `${ENV_VAR}` placeholders; local (default) and user scope live in `~/.claude.json`; secrets never go into version control.
Bearer tokens go in an `Authorization` header; remote servers that need sign-in use OAuth 2.0 through `/mcp`; the connector takes `authorization_token`.
Tool descriptions drive selection: purpose, when to use, inputs, outputs and how it differs from similar tools; merge overlapping tools and namespace by service.
Selection accuracy drops past 30 to 50 tools; tool search with `defer_loading` loads 3 to 5 on demand and cuts definition tokens by over 85%.
Failures return `is_error: true` with category, retryable flag and next steps; an empty search is a success; client tools run in your app, server tools on Anthropic's side.
traps: Fixing wrong-tool selection with a longer system prompt or a bigger model instead of sharper descriptions and fewer overlapping tools.
Returning an empty string or a generic failure message, so the agent invents data or retries the same call.
Hard-coding bearer tokens or API keys in a committed config instead of environment-variable references or OAuth.

notes.objective: Design multi-tool agent workflows that coordinate access to specialized MCP tools for distinct operational domains (e.g., CRM, billing, code repositories).
notes.title: MCP servers: primitives and transports
notes.gist: One MCP server exposes tools, resources and prompts to any MCP client, and the transport follows where the server runs.
points: Tools are model-invoked actions; resources are data you reference by URI (`@server:protocol://path`) that Claude Code fetches as attachments; prompts are user-run templates that appear as `/mcp__server__prompt` commands.
Use resources for static catalogs, policy libraries or schemas that applications inject as context, and tools for actions that change state or need parameters (submit a report, process a refund).
stdio runs the server as a local subprocess over stdin and stdout, so diagnostics must go to stderr or they corrupt the protocol stream; choose HTTP when one central server serves many remote users.
Streamable HTTP is the recommended remote transport; SSE is deprecated, and a WebSocket server supports header authentication only.

A capability needed by Claude Desktop, Claude Code and in-house apps belongs in one maintained MCP server, not a copy per application; a Skill packages instructions and scripts but is not a persistent authenticated connection.
notes.tip: 'Three apps need the same inventory service' means one MCP server exposing tools; 'logging breaks a local server' means print to stderr; 'users launch parameterized queries from a menu' means MCP prompts.

flowchart TB
  A[MCP server] --> B[Tools: actions]
  A --> C[Resources: data to reference]
  A --> D[Prompts: user templates]
  B --> E[Any MCP client]
  C --> E
  D --> E

notes.objective: Configure and authenticate custom MCP servers with Claude agents, including bearer token authentication and API credential management.
notes.title: Configure and authenticate MCP servers
notes.gist: Pick the scope, keep tokens out of version control, and use headers or OAuth for remote authentication.
points: `claude mcp add --transport http` or `stdio` registers a server; the default local scope lives in `~/.claude.json` (private, current project), project scope writes a shared `.mcp.json` at the repo root, user scope spans all your projects.

Share team servers with `--scope project` and commit `.mcp.json`; `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}` expand environment variables, so `Authorization: Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}` keeps the token in CI and developer environments, not in git.

Bearer or API-key auth for HTTP servers goes in `headers` (or `--header`); servers that answer 401 or 403 and support OAuth 2.0 are signed in per user through `/mcp`, which beats everyone pasting personal keys.

Through the Messages API, the MCP connector takes `mcp_servers` entries (`type` of `url`, an `https://` URL, a `name`, optional `authorization_token`) plus an `mcp_toolset` in `tools` to allow or deny tools; only tool calls work, and the server must be publicly reachable, not stdio.
Debug with `/mcp` status and the MCP Inspector, which calls tools directly and shows protocol messages; a server marked failed or needing auth can leave Claude quietly falling back to built-in tools.
notes.tip: 'The config must be shared without secrets' means `--scope project` plus `${ENV}` placeholders; 'only one developer can see the server' means it sits in local scope; 'the API should handle the connection, no MCP client of ours' means the connector's `mcp_servers` field.

flowchart TB

  A -->|Whole team| C[Project scope in .mcp.json]
  A -->|All my projects| D[User scope]
  C --> E[Secrets via env var placeholders]
