notes.objective: Design multi-tool agent workflows that coordinate access to specialized MCP tools for distinct operational domains (e.g., CRM, billing, code repositories).
notes.title: Design tools agents choose correctly
notes.gist: Selection quality comes from clear, distinct tools and descriptions, not from longer system prompts.
points: The description is the biggest lever: say what the tool does, in which situations to call it and when not to, what each parameter means and what comes back, in enough detail to separate it from similar tools (three or four sentences is the floor).

Consolidate and namespace: replace `list_users`, `list_events` and `create_event` with one `schedule_event`, prefix by service (`asana_search`, `jira_search`), and delete overlapping tools; overlap makes the model pick the wrong one.

Constrain inputs in the schema: `enum` for allowed states, `required` for must-have fields, unambiguous names such as `user_id`; strict mode guarantees conformance, and schema rules beat prompt warnings.

Return high-signal output: names beside IDs, only the fields the next step needs, pagination or truncation (Claude Code caps tool output at 25,000 tokens by default) and a `response_format` switch between concise and detailed.

Prove it with evaluations: realistic multi-step tasks with verifiable answers, tracking accuracy, tool-call counts, errors and tokens; when a new MCP server lowers success, check overlap with existing tools first.
notes.tip: 'Claude keeps calling the account tool for billing questions' means rewrite both descriptions with boundaries; 'forty overlapping tools' means consolidate; 'invalid status strings' means an enum in the schema.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Wrong tool chosen] --> B{Why?}
  B -->|Vague descriptions| C[Rewrite purpose, limits, parameters]
  B -->|Overlapping tools| D[Merge and namespace]
  B -->|Free-text values| E[Enum and required fields]

notes.objective: Implement error handling and fallback strategies when MCP tools return incomplete or unreliable data in production agent systems.
notes.title: Tool errors and unreliable data
notes.gist: Tell the agent what failed and what to do next, and keep empty results distinct from failures.
points: Report a failed call as a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` (MCP `isError: true`) and an instructive message; the model adapts in the same turn, whereas a fresh user message about the failure derails the loop.

Return structure the agent can act on: error category (transient, validation, business rule, permission), a retryable flag, what was attempted and a customer-safe message; a generic 'failed' or an empty string pushes the agent to invent data or retry blindly.
A confirmed empty search is a successful result and a timeout is an error; keep them distinct so an outage is not read as 'no records'.

Retry only transient failures, with backoff and a cap; fix arguments for validation errors, explain the policy for business-rule errors, escalate permission errors; Claude retries an invalid call 2 to 3 times with corrections before apologizing.

With incomplete or conflicting data, return what was found plus the explicit gap, mark the claim unverified, use a fallback source or cached summary, and escalate to a person below your confidence threshold; with parallel calls return the successes and flag only the failed one.
notes.tip: 'The agent invents data or repeats the same failed query' usually traces to a tool returning an empty string on failure; the fix is a detailed error with category and retry guidance, not a stronger prompt.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Tool call fails or data incomplete] --> B{Failure type?}
  B -->|Transient| C[Retry with backoff, then fallback]
  B -->|Validation| D[Return error with fix hints]
  B -->|Permission or policy| E[Explain and escalate]

notes.objective: Develop agent-based solutions that decompose complex customer service requests into independent sub-tasks and route them to appropriate MCP tools.
notes.title: Decompose and route to the right tools
notes.gist: Split a multi-issue request into independent concerns, give each the tools it needs, and keep large catalogs out of context.
points: Verify the customer first, then decompose the request into independent concerns (a return, a billing error, an account problem), investigate them in parallel with the verified context shared, and merge the findings into one reply.
Route by domain: billing tools to a billing specialist, CRM tools to an account specialist; the coordinator activates only the specialists whose tool descriptions match the issue.
Parallel tool calls arrive as several `tool_use` blocks in one turn; set `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` inside `tool_choice` when two calls could modify the same record.

Past 30 to 50 tools, selection accuracy drops and definitions bloat context (a five-server setup can cost about 55k tokens); tool search with `defer_loading: true` loads 3 to 5 relevant tools on demand and cuts definition tokens by over 85%.
Dependent steps (lookup, then refund) stay sequential and the refund tool is gated until verification passes; `tool_choice` of `any` guarantees some tool call when a request must be routed to a tool.
notes.tip: 'Several independent issues in one message' means decompose and run in parallel with shared context; 'two tool_use blocks update the same record' means `disable_parallel_tool_use`; 'ninety integrations and wrong picks' means merge them and use tool search.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Verify the customer] --> B[Split into independent concerns]
  B --> C[Specialist per domain in parallel]
  C --> D[Combine findings]
  D --> E[One unified reply]

notes.objective: Build multi-agent systems using the Claude Agent SDK where specialized sub-agents delegate tasks to a coordinator agent and integrate with MCP servers.
notes.title: Subagents with scoped MCP access
notes.gist: Give each subagent only its own domain's MCP tools and keep high-risk tools with the coordinator.
points: Scope MCP access per subagent: its `tools` list names `mcp__server__tool` entries, `mcpServers` on the definition attaches servers to that agent, and `disallowedTools` can remove a whole server with `mcp__server__*`.
Keep high-risk tools such as `submit_refund_request` or `route_to_specialist` with the coordinator, and delegate read-only lookups to specialists.
Results flow up, not sideways: subagents return structured findings to the coordinator, which decides the next step; workers do not message peers or build deep chains.
Compose servers by source: a community MCP server for standard needs (a bug tracker) plus a small custom one for proprietary logic; register shared servers in `.mcp.json` and personal ones per user.

In-process tools are MCP too: `create_sdk_mcp_server` wraps `tool()` handlers; `readOnlyHint: true` lets Claude run them in parallel, while `destructiveHint`, `idempotentHint` and `openWorldHint` are informational only.
notes.tip: 'The subagent can call tools it should not' means list its `tools` explicitly, because omitting the field inherits everything; 'delegation announced but nothing happens' means `Agent` is missing from `allowedTools`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Coordinator] --> B[Billing subagent, billing tools]
  A --> C[Account subagent, CRM tools]
  B --> D[Findings back to coordinator]
  C --> D

notes.objective: Integrate Claude agents with code analysis and repository navigation tools via MCP to enable automated code review, architecture understanding, and template generation.
notes.title: Code and repo tools via MCP
notes.gist: Let the agent find files by pattern, read only what it needs, and reach repository systems through MCP.
points: Navigate cheaply: `Glob` finds files by name pattern (for example `**/*.config.yaml`), `Grep` finds content by regex, then `Read` only the matches; reading the whole repository exhausts the token budget.
Search before changing: grep for the exact string (such as a renamed field) across the repo, trace callers and imports, and read the tests, instead of guessing from file names.
Delegate exploration: the built-in `Explore` subagent, a fast read-only agent, searches in its own context and returns a summary, keeping the main window for the change.
Reach repository systems through MCP servers (GitHub for pull requests and issues, a code-search or docs server); give the review agent read-only tools and a schema for its findings.

For templates and refactors, read existing examples first, plan before multi-file changes, and use `Edit` for targeted replacements; when the anchor text is not unique, read the file and rewrite it with `Write`.
notes.tip: 'Locate every config file under any directory' wants `Glob`; 'find where customer_identifier is used' wants `Grep` for the exact string; 'exploration fills the main context' wants an Explore subagent.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Understand or change code] --> B[Glob candidate files]
  B --> C[Grep exact strings]
  C --> D[Read only the matches]
  D --> E[Summarize or edit]

cards.q: What are the three MCP primitives?
cards.a: Tools are actions the model calls; resources are data you reference by URI; prompts are parameterized templates a user runs.

cards.q: A local stdio MCP server breaks after print statements are added. Why, and what is the fix?
cards.a: A stdio server speaks the protocol over stdout, so stray output corrupts it. Send diagnostics to stderr.

cards.q: Which MCP transport serves dozens of remote team members from one central server?
cards.a: Streamable HTTP. stdio is a local subprocess, and SSE is deprecated.

cards.q: Where do the local, project and user MCP scopes store servers, and which is shared with the team?
cards.a: Local and user live in `~/.claude.json`. Project uses `.mcp.json` in the repo root, committed and shared.

cards.q: How do you share an authenticated MCP server config in git without leaking the token?
cards.a: Use project scope with `Authorization: Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}` in `.mcp.json`, and set the variable in CI and in each developer's environment.

cards.q: How do remote MCP servers that need sign-in authenticate each user?
cards.a: With OAuth 2.0 through `/mcp` (servers answering 401 or 403 are flagged), rather than everyone pasting personal API keys into config.

cards.q: What does the Messages API MCP connector need, and what can it not do?
cards.a: An `mcp_servers` entry (HTTPS URL, name, optional `authorization_token`) plus an `mcp_toolset` in `tools`. Tool calls only; no local stdio servers.

cards.q: What matters most for whether Claude calls the right tool?
cards.a: Clear descriptions: what it does, when to use it and when not, and what each parameter means, distinct from similar tools.

cards.q: An MCP server exposes forty overlapping tools and the model picks wrongly. What is the fix?
cards.a: Consolidate and namespace the tools so each has a distinct purpose, and sharpen the descriptions.

cards.q: A backend accepts five action states but Claude sends free text. How do you stop that?
cards.a: Define the parameter as a schema enum of the allowed states, mark must-have fields required, and add strict mode for guaranteed conformance.

cards.q: How should a tool report that its backend call timed out?
cards.a: A `tool_result` with `is_error: true` plus category, retryable flag and next steps. Never an empty string; a confirmed empty search stays a success.

cards.q: Two parallel tool_use blocks try to modify the same record. What setting prevents this?
cards.a: `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` inside the `tool_choice` object, which limits Claude to one tool call per turn under auto.

cards.q: At what tool count does selection accuracy degrade, and what is the fix?
cards.a: Beyond about 30 to 50 tools. Use tool search with `defer_loading: true`; it loads 3 to 5 tools on demand and cuts definition tokens by over 85%.

cards.q: Which tool types run on Anthropic's infrastructure and which run in your application?
cards.a: Server tools (web search, web fetch, code execution, tool search) run on Anthropic's side. Custom tools, bash, text editor and computer use run in your app.

cards.q: Which built-in tools find repository files cheaply before anything is read?
cards.a: `Glob` matches file names by pattern, `Grep` searches content by regex, then `Read` only the matches; an Explore subagent can do the searching.

summary.tests: Whether you can keep an agent inside safe bounds: least-privilege tools, deterministic hooks, injection-resistant design, human approval for risky actions, honest handling of uncertain data and audit trails.
must_know: Make forbidden actions impossible: remove the tool or credential; permissions run hooks, deny, ask, mode, allow, then `canUseTool`, and a hook deny holds even in `bypassPermissions`.
Hard rules (refund limits, identity match, protected paths, destructive commands) belong in `PreToolUse` hooks or tool code, never only in prompts or CLAUDE.md.
Third-party content is untrusted data: put it in `tool_result`, label and delimit it, and remove or gate the dangerous tool; model output is untrusted too, so escape, parameterize and validate it.
Irreversible or financial actions go to a human through `canUseTool`, a hook `ask` or `defer`, or a threshold queue, with a structured handoff of customer, root cause and actions tried.
Missing values are null and conflicts are escalated with both sources; ambiguous identity means asking for an identifier, not guessing.
Audit every tool call with `tool_use_id`, the API `request-id`, the decision source and blocked attempts; OpenTelemetry events redact prompts by default.
Keys stay on the backend in a secrets manager, one per environment or service; a leaked key is revoked and rotated; workspaces isolate teams with their own limits.
traps: Adding a stronger system-prompt warning to stop an injection or a risky action instead of removing the capability or adding a hook.
Putting an API key in the system prompt, client app or URL so Claude can pass it to a tool.
Letting an agent resolve conflicting or missing data by guessing, or escalating on customer frustration alone.

notes.objective: Implement access controls and tool permissions to restrict agent capabilities to only necessary functions and prevent unauthorized operations on sensitive systems.
notes.title: Least privilege for agent tools
notes.gist: Give an agent only the tools and credentials its job needs, and make forbidden capabilities absent rather than discouraged.
points: Naming a whole tool such as `Bash` in `disallowedTools` takes it out of the request, so Claude cannot even attempt it; a scoped rule like `Bash(rm *)` is denied in every mode, including `bypassPermissions`.

Pair `allowedTools` of read-only tools with `permissionMode` of `dontAsk` for a locked-down headless agent: listed tools run and everything else is denied; `allowedTools` does not constrain `bypassPermissions`, which approves every tool.

Split a catch-all tool (arbitrary SQL with admin rights) into narrow tools that expose only the read operations needed, backed by a least-privilege credential; an agent that summarizes URLs must simply not hold the refund tool.
Pre-approve with scoped rules, not bare tool names: `Bash(npm test *)` approves only matching commands and everything else still falls through to the mode, `canUseTool` or a denial.
Run unattended jobs in a sandbox or disposable environment with limited filesystem and network access; managed settings enforce organization policy that developers cannot weaken locally.
notes.tip: 'Must never be able to' calls for removing the capability (no tool, no credential, a deny rule), not an instruction in the prompt; 'subagents bypass the safety constraints' points to per-subagent `tools` and coordinator oversight.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Job description] --> B[List only the tools it needs]
  B --> C[Scope credentials narrowly]
  C --> D[Deny everything else]
  D --> E[Sandbox unattended runs]

notes.objective: Design multi-agent systems with clear delegation boundaries and coordinator oversight to ensure subagents operate within approved scopes and cannot bypass safety constraints.
notes.title: Delegation boundaries and coordinator oversight
notes.gist: Each subagent gets a narrow scope in code, and the coordinator keeps sight of everything it delegates.
points: Scope each subagent in its definition: `tools` is the allowlist (omit it and the subagent inherits every tool), `disallowedTools` removes more, and `mcpServers` attaches only its own servers; a tool left out is absent, not merely discouraged.

Permission mode flows down: a subagent runs in the parent's mode, can be made stricter with `permissionMode` when the parent is in default, `dontAsk` or `plan`, and never receives `bypassPermissions` unless the parent has it.

Hooks fire inside subagents too (hook inputs carry `agent_id` and `agent_type`), so one `PreToolUse` guard covers the whole tree, and `SubagentStart` and `SubagentStop` record who was spawned and what came back.
Cap the tree: nesting depth (default 3 layers, `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` of 1 stops it), concurrency (default 20) and `max_budget_usd`; at a limit new spawns are refused.

Coordinator oversight: risky tools stay with the coordinator, workers return findings and errors to it instead of messaging each other, and Claude Code scans a subagent's final message for instruction-shaped text before the parent reads it.
notes.tip: 'Subagents bypass the safety constraints' points to per-subagent `tools`, inherited permissions and hooks that run everywhere; 'a worker spawned its own children' points to depth caps and coordinator-only spawning.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Coordinator holds risky tools] --> B[Subagent with allowlisted tools]
  B --> C[Hooks and deny rules still apply]
  C --> D[Findings return to the coordinator]
  A --> E[Depth, concurrency and budget caps]

notes.objective: Implement access controls and tool permissions to restrict agent capabilities to only necessary functions and prevent unauthorized operations on sensitive systems.
notes.title: Enforce hard rules in hooks and tool code
notes.gist: Anything that must always or never happen belongs in code that runs on every tool call.
points: Permissions are checked in this order: hooks, deny rules, ask rules, the permission mode, allow rules, then `canUseTool`; a `PreToolUse` hook runs first and its `deny` holds even in `bypassPermissions`.

`PreToolUse` returns `allow`, `deny`, `ask` or `defer` (deny beats defer beats ask beats allow) plus a reason Claude reads; use it to block forced pushes, `rm -rf`, writes to `.env` or protected paths, secrets in file content, and Bash commands outside a safe zone.

Hard business limits live in tool code or middleware: reject `process_refund` over a threshold and tell the agent to call `escalate_to_human`, require the customer ID to equal the order owner ID, and end with a catch-all that denies anything not explicitly approved.
A matcher scopes a hook to named tools (`Write|Edit`), so a Bash write to the same file bypasses it; cover Bash as well or sandbox it.
Validate arguments inside the tool: parameterize SQL, resolve and check file paths, and pass the authenticated user's ID from the session to every tool so authorization is not left to the model.
notes.tip: 'Skips the check about 5 percent of the time' or 'ignored the documented rule' means deterministic enforcement in a hook or tool; 'a crafted amount reaches the database query' means parameterize inside the tool.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Tool call requested] --> B{PreToolUse hook}
  B -->|deny| C[Blocked with a reason]
  B -->|ask| D[Wait for human confirmation]
  B -->|allow| E[Deny and allow rules, then run]

notes.objective: Validate and sanitize all inputs and outputs in agent workflows to prevent injection attacks, data leakage, and misuse of tool results across agent handoffs.
notes.title: Prompt injection and untrusted content
notes.gist: Third-party text is data, never instructions: separate it, label it, and make sure a successful injection can do little.
points: Direct injection and jailbreaks come from the user; indirect injection hides instructions in emails, web pages, documents, database rows or tool results while the user is trusted.

Deliver third-party content only inside `tool_result` blocks, state what it is and where it came from, JSON-encode or tag-delimit it, and tell Claude in the system prompt that such content is data that never overrides instructions.

Do not rely on wording alone: least privilege (remove or gate the email or refund tool), sandboxes, approval for high-risk actions, and an optional small-model screen (Haiku with structured output) of tool results before Claude acts.

Against direct attacks pre-screen input with a lightweight classifier or pattern validation, harden the system prompt with refusal rules, throttle or ban repeat offenders, and red-team with injected documents before launch.
Treat model output as untrusted too: escape it before rendering in a page, parameterize any SQL, validate against a schema, and redact patterns such as account numbers in a post-generation filter.
notes.tip: 'Hidden text in a page or email makes the agent act' is a capability problem: remove or gate the dangerous tool and separate data from instructions; 'write a stricter system prompt' alone is the distractor.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Email or web page] --> B[Inside tool_result, labeled untrusted]
  B --> C[Claude reads it as data]
  C --> D{Action needs a sensitive tool?}
  D -->|Yes| E[Gate or deny the tool]
  D -->|No| F[Answer the user]

notes.objective: Implement human escalation checkpoints and approval workflows for high-risk agent actions such as financial transactions, refunds, and account modifications.
notes.title: Human checkpoints for high-risk actions
notes.gist: Pause irreversible or financial actions for a person, in code, with a structured handoff.
points: Gate refunds, transfers, account changes, instance termination and firewall edits behind human approval; threshold rules (refunds over a limit, expenses over $5,000) intercept the `tool_use` and send it to a human queue instead of executing it.

The `canUseTool` callback asks a person (approve, approve with changed input, reject with a message), a `PreToolUse` hook can return `ask` or `defer` to wait or resume later, and `plan` mode proposes changes without executing them.

Prefer `ask` over a hard block when legitimate work needs sensitive access, so a person can confirm instead of the session failing; a `PermissionRequest` hook can notify Slack or email while Claude waits.

Hand off through a required-schema escalation tool: customer ID, verified status, root cause, actions already tried, recommended next step; escalate on explicit request, policy gaps or no progress, not on customer frustration alone.
Earn autonomy: start in read-only or simulation mode that logs intended actions, review approval rates by output type, and cut review only for categories that stay reliable.
notes.tip: 'Policy mandates review above a threshold but the agent sometimes approves anyway' means intercept in code and route to a queue; 'legitimate reports need access to sensitive tables' means ask for confirmation rather than terminate.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Agent proposes an action] --> B{High risk or over threshold?}
  B -->|No| C[Run and log it]
  B -->|Yes| D[Pause for human approval]
  D --> E{Approved?}
  E -->|Yes| C
  E -->|No| F[Escalate with structured handoff]

notes.objective: Configure agents to detect and handle discrepancies, conflicts, and anomalies in data before taking autonomous action, with escalation when confidence thresholds are not met.
notes.title: Detect conflicts and uncertainty before acting
notes.gist: Let the agent say it does not know, flag discrepancies, and stop for review instead of guessing.
points: Allow 'I don't know': explicit permission to admit uncertainty cuts false information; for long documents extract word-for-word quotes first, and make claims auditable with citations, retracting any claim without a supporting quote.
Missing data is null, not invented: tell Claude absent values must be null, and stop retrying when validation shows the source lacks the field; mark the record incomplete and request the document.
Treat ambiguous identity as unresolved: ask for an account number or email before lookups or actions, and keep the refund tool blocked until the verified customer ID matches the order owner.

Flag conflicts instead of resolving them silently: when form data disagrees with the record, return a schema-validated escalation packet naming both values and sources; mark a claim with no textual support as unverified.

Raise confidence with checks: best-of-N runs that disagree signal hallucination, an independent reviewer session sees only the source and a rubric, and below a set confidence threshold the case escalates.
notes.tip: 'The model invents a phone number or ticket id' means null plus an instruction (and a nullable schema); 'form and record disagree' means escalate with both values, never merge; 'confidence below threshold' means a human queue.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Extracted or retrieved data] --> B{Missing, ambiguous or conflicting?}
  B -->|Missing| C[Null and request the source]
  B -->|Ambiguous| D[Ask for an identifier]
  B -->|Conflicting| E[Escalate with both values]
  B -->|Clean| F[Proceed to the action]

notes.objective: Establish audit logging and monitoring for all agent tool calls and decisions to enable post-incident analysis and compliance verification of autonomous system behavior.
notes.title: Audit logging and monitoring
notes.gist: Record every tool call and decision with enough identifiers to reconstruct what the agent did and why.
points: Log each tool call with tool name, inputs, result or error, duration, who or what approved it, session and agent IDs and timestamps; blocked attempts count too, so a denying `PreToolUse` hook should persist the attempt.

Hooks are the deterministic capture points: `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` for every call, `SubagentStart` and `SubagentStop` for delegation, `PermissionRequest` for approvals; an async hook can ship events to a logging service without slowing the loop.

Correlate with identifiers: the API `request-id` header, the `tool_use_id` (also passed to hooks) and, in Claude Code OpenTelemetry events, `tool_result` with its `decision_source` (config, hook or user).

Claude Code exports metrics and events through OpenTelemetry; prompt text and tool details stay redacted unless you opt in (`OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS`, `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS`), and managed settings can pin the collector so developers cannot redirect it.

Track cost and access per workspace with separate keys and spend limits, and send an opaque `metadata.user_id` so abuse can be traced; keep prompts in version control and record the model version per environment.
notes.tip: 'Post-incident analysis' or 'compliance verification' wants durable per-call records with IDs and decisions, including denials; never log secrets or raw sensitive prompts.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Agent tool call] --> B[PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks]
  B --> C[Structured audit event with IDs]
  C --> D[Central log store]
  D --> E[Alerts and incident review]

notes.objective: Validate and sanitize all inputs and outputs in agent workflows to prevent injection attacks, data leakage, and misuse of tool results across agent handoffs.
notes.title: Secrets, data handling and tenant isolation
notes.gist: Keep keys and sensitive data out of prompts and clients, and keep each tenant's context separate.
points: API keys never go in client-side code, URLs or the system prompt: call Claude from a backend, send the key in a header, load it from a secrets manager at runtime, and use separate keys per environment and per service so one leak is contained.
A leaked key stays valid even after the commit is rolled back: deactivate it in the Console and issue a new one; ZDR organizations cannot use CORS, so browser apps must go through a backend proxy.
Isolate by workspace: one workspace per business unit or contractor group, each with its own keys, spend and rate limits and role assignments; the default workspace cannot have spend limits.

Keep sensitive data out of the model's reach: mask or remove identifiers client-side before the request, keep proprietary formulas and secrets in backend logic, and use ZDR or a cloud-provider route where policy requires data to stay inside.

Tenant isolation: separate stored conversations, retrieved documents and caches per tenant, derive the user from the authenticated session (never from the prompt), and tag requests with an opaque `metadata.user_id`.
notes.tip: 'The key was embedded in the mobile app' means a backend service plus revoke and rotate; 'one team's burst depleted the shared quota' means separate workspaces with limits; 'another organization's details appeared' means tenant-scoped storage and retrieval.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Client app] --> B[Your backend with a secrets manager]
  B --> C[Claude API with a per-service key]
  B --> D[Tenant-scoped data only]
  C --> E[Workspace limits and logs]

cards.q: What happens when a deny rule names a bare tool such as `Bash` in `disallowedTools`?
cards.a: The tool is stripped from the request, so Claude cannot see or attempt it. A scoped rule like `Bash(rm *)` is denied in every mode.

cards.q: In what order does the Agent SDK evaluate permissions?
cards.a: Hooks first, then deny rules, ask rules, the permission mode, allow rules and finally the `canUseTool` callback. A hook deny holds even in `bypassPermissions`.

cards.q: Does `allowedTools` with only `Read` restrict an agent running in `bypassPermissions` mode?
cards.a: No. Unlisted tools fall through to the mode, which approves everything. Use `disallowedTools` or a hook to block tools there.

cards.q: What does a subagent inherit about permissions, and how do you keep it inside its scope?
cards.a: It runs in the parent's permission mode and never gets `bypassPermissions` unless the parent has it. List only its own tools; omitting the field inherits every tool.

cards.q: An agent sometimes processes refunds above policy despite instructions. What is the fix?
cards.a: Intercept `process_refund` in a hook or middleware, reject amounts over the limit and route the case to `escalate_to_human`. Prompts alone are unreliable.

cards.q: A hook with matcher `Write|Edit` blocks writes to `.env`. How can Claude still change the file?
cards.a: With a Bash command, which that matcher does not cover. Cover Bash as well or run commands in a sandbox.

cards.q: How do you keep third-party content from acting as instructions?
cards.a: Deliver it only in `tool_result` blocks, label its source, JSON-encode or tag-delimit it, say in the system prompt it is data, and gate sensitive tools.

cards.q: A fetched web page tells the agent to email the conversation to an address. What is the effective defense?
cards.a: Treat the page as untrusted data and remove or approval-gate the email tool, so injected text cannot trigger sending.

cards.q: Model output is rendered into a web page or used in a SQL query. What must the application do?
cards.a: Treat it as untrusted: escape or sanitize it before rendering, and parameterize arguments inside the tool before any database query.

cards.q: How do you enforce human review for expenses over $5,000?
cards.a: Intercept the `tool_use` above the threshold in code and route it to a human queue before execution. A prompt rule is not enough.

cards.q: Name the fields of a good escalation handoff.
cards.a: Customer ID, verified status, root cause, actions already tried and a recommended next step, passed through a required-schema escalation tool.

cards.q: A form lacks a phone number and the model fabricates one. What is the fix?
cards.a: Instruct Claude that missing values must be null and make the field nullable; stop retrying when the source lacks the data and request the document.

cards.q: Where should API keys live, and what do you do after one leaks?
cards.a: On a backend, loaded from a secrets manager, one key per environment or service. After a leak, deactivate it in the Console and issue a new one.

cards.q: How do you isolate cost and access for several business units in one organization?
cards.a: Give each unit its own workspace with its own API keys, spend and rate limits, and role assignments.

cards.q: Which identifiers correlate an incident across API logs, hooks and Claude Code telemetry?
cards.a: The API `request-id`, the `tool_use_id` (also passed to hooks and present on `tool_result` events), and the decision source.

summary.tests: Whether you can configure and drive Claude Code and the Agent SDK for real engineering work: shared conventions, headless CI, economical code search, plan versus direct mode, structured review output and safe refactors.
must_know: Shared conventions go in a committed `CLAUDE.md` (root or `.claude/`), personal ones in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` or `CLAUDE.local.md`; path-scoped `.claude/rules/` and skills load on demand.
Reusable commands live in `.claude/commands/` or `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (frontmatter `context: fork`, `allowed-tools`, `argument-hint`) and are committed so CI and teammates get them.
CLAUDE.md is advisory while hooks are deterministic: a PostToolUse hook runs the formatter, a PreToolUse hook blocks, and only exit code 2 (or a deny decision) stops an action.
Find code with Glob, then Grep exact strings, then Read only the matches; delegate exploration to a subagent so the main context stays small.
Use plan mode for multi-file, architectural or unfamiliar work, and direct execution when the diff fits in one sentence.
In CI use `claude -p` with `--output-format json` and `--json-schema`; `--resume` and `--continue` restore sessions and `fork_session` branches one.
Before refactoring thin-coverage code write characterization tests, then refactor one subsystem per branch and verify after each step.
traps: Relying on CLAUDE.md or a prompt for a step that must always run, instead of a hook.
Letting Claude read whole directories to find a string instead of using Glob and Grep.
Entering plan mode for a one-line fix, or skipping it for a cross-service refactor.

notes.objective: Build code assistance agents using the Claude Agent SDK that integrate with MCP services and execute tools like file reading, writing, code search, and test execution.
notes.title: Build a code assistant with the Agent SDK
notes.gist: The Agent SDK gives you Claude Code's loop, tools and context handling as a library, so you configure rather than rebuild them.
points: `query()` runs the agent loop with built-in tools (`Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Glob`, `Grep`, `Bash`, `WebSearch`), permissions, hooks, subagents, MCP and sessions; the Client SDK leaves the loop to you.

Options that matter: `allowedTools` to auto-approve, `mcpServers` for external systems, `agents` for subagents (add `Agent` to `allowedTools`), `settingSources` to load CLAUDE.md, rules and skills, and `max_turns` plus `max_budget_usd` as limits.
Test execution runs through `Bash`; give the agent a check it can run (tests, linter, build) and have it iterate until the check passes, showing the output as evidence.
Project guidance reaches an SDK agent only through loaded setting sources, so a `CLAUDE.md` is ignored when the `project` source is off; custom tools run as in-process MCP tools.
From other languages or scripts, drive the same loop as a subprocess with `claude -p`; authenticate with an API key, since third parties may not offer claude.ai login.
notes.tip: 'An agent that reads files, searches code and runs tests' points to the Agent SDK with built-in tools rather than a hand-built Messages API loop; 'the agent ignores our CLAUDE.md' means the setting sources were not loaded.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Prompt] --> B[query with allowedTools and mcpServers]
  B --> C[Agent loop runs the tools]
  C --> D[Tests run as the check]
  D --> E[ResultMessage]

notes.objective: Design agents that navigate and comprehend large, complex codebases by strategically reading files and gathering context without exhausting token budgets.
notes.title: Read a large codebase economically
notes.gist: Search narrowly first, read only the matches, and push noisy exploration into subagents.
points: `Glob` finds candidate files by name pattern (`*refund*.yaml`, `**/*.config.yaml`), `Grep` finds an exact error string or function name by regex across contents, and `Read` opens only those files; never read whole directories.

Go from broad to narrow: an overview, then the key data models, then one feature's flow; reference files with `@`, and tell Claude what you see, where you think it lives and how you will know it is fixed.
Delegate research: 'use subagents to investigate X' runs it in a separate context and returns a summary; the built-in Explore agent is a fast read-only searcher.

Persist findings outside the window: a short findings or progress file the agent re-reads each step; `/clear` between unrelated tasks, `/compact` with instructions, and `--continue` or `--resume` to return to a session.
The failure pattern is an unscoped 'investigate': hundreds of files read, context full and quality falling; scope the question or use a subagent.
notes.tip: 'Locate every file matching a naming convention' wants Glob; 'find callers of a renamed function' wants Grep with the exact string; 'exploration is filling the context' wants a subagent or a notes file.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Question] --> B[Glob by name pattern]
  B --> C[Grep the exact string]
  C --> D[Read only the matches]
  D --> E[Notes or summary]

notes.objective: Configure Claude Code with custom commands and CLAUDE.md settings to enforce team-specific patterns for testing, error handling, module organization, and code review workflows.
notes.title: Team conventions: CLAUDE.md, rules, commands
notes.gist: Commit shared guidance to the repo, keep personal preferences local, and load specialist guidance only where it applies.
points: A committed `CLAUDE.md` (root or `.claude/`) is the team standard for testing, error handling and module layout, and every clone loads it; `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` holds personal style and `CLAUDE.local.md` project-local preferences.

In a monorepo keep the root file small, give each service a short CLAUDE.md that `@path`-imports the authoritative standards, and use `.claude/rules/*.md` with `paths` globs for test files, migrations or generated clients so they load only when matching files are touched.

Custom slash commands live in `.claude/commands/` (committed with the repo); skills in `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` are the richer form, with `description`, `argument-hint`, `allowed-tools`, `disable-model-invocation` and `context: fork` frontmatter, and personal skills go in `~/.claude/skills/`.
A skill with `context: fork` does its heavy reading in its own subagent context and returns a concise summary; a skill beats a command of the same name, and enterprise beats personal beats project.
`/init` drafts a CLAUDE.md and `/context` lists the memory files that loaded; keep each file under about 200 lines and review it like code.
notes.tip: 'New hires get different suggestions than seniors' means a committed project CLAUDE.md; 'the command must exist in CI' means commit it under `.claude/`, not `~/.claude`; 'investigate a ticket in isolation with read-only tools' means a skill with `context: fork`.

flowchart TB
  A{Who needs the guidance?} -->|Whole team| B[Committed CLAUDE.md]
  A -->|Only me| C[User CLAUDE.md or local file]
  A -->|Some file paths| D[Rules file with paths]
  A -->|A repeatable workflow| E[Command or skill]

notes.objective: Configure Claude Code with custom commands and CLAUDE.md settings to enforce team-specific patterns for testing, error handling, module organization, and code review workflows.
notes.title: Hooks and settings: make it deterministic
notes.gist: CLAUDE.md is advisory; hooks and settings are enforced, and each has a scope and a precedence.
points: A `PostToolUse` hook on `Edit|Write` runs a formatter or linter after every modification; a `PreToolUse` hook can block edits to a protected directory or dangerous Bash patterns.
Hook exit codes: 0 succeeds, 2 is a blocking error whose stderr is the reason Claude reads, and any other code (including 1) is a non-blocking error that does not stop the action.

Settings scopes: `.claude/settings.json` is shared and committed (team permissions and hooks), `.claude/settings.local.json` is personal and git-ignored, `~/.claude/settings.json` applies to all your projects.

Precedence from highest: managed settings, the `--settings` flag, project local, shared project, user; list keys such as `permissions.allow` merge across files, and nothing local overrides a managed key.
Permission rules live in settings: a `deny` rule for `Bash(docker push *)` blocks that command and an `allow` rule for `Bash(npm run build)` pre-approves one.
notes.tip: 'Must lint after every change' or 'must never touch this directory' means hooks, not CLAUDE.md; 'the hook prints a warning but the command still runs' means it exited 1 instead of 2.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Claude edits a file] --> B[PostToolUse hook runs the formatter]
  B --> C{Exit code?}
  C -->|0| D[Continue]
  C -->|2| E[Blocking error, stderr to Claude]

notes.objective: Implement agents that perform code analysis and debugging by correlating production errors with source code to identify root causes in complex systems.
notes.title: Debug by correlating errors with code
notes.gist: Give Claude the exact symptom, search for its literal string, trace the path and prove the fix with a failing test.
points: Provide the error text, the command that reproduces it, the stack trace and whether it is intermittent; a bare 'fix the bug' wastes turns.
Grep the exact error string and the handler or function names, then Read the matching files; follow callers and service or queue boundaries instead of guessing from file names.
Trace the path end to end (front end to database, producer to consumer) and compare code, configuration and recent changes; filter logs rather than loading them whole.
Write a test that fails because of the bug, fix the root cause rather than suppressing the error, and rerun the test so the check closes the loop.

In distributed systems give each subagent one service or log source and require findings with file paths, line ranges and excerpts, then correlate them in the coordinator; report blocked paths separately from empty results.
notes.tip: 'DatabaseConnectionPoolExhausted in production logs' wants Grep on that exact string plus the function names; 'the fix suppresses the error' is the trap; success needs a test that fails before and passes after.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Error message and repro steps] --> B[Grep the exact string]
  B --> C[Read matching files and callers]
  C --> D[Failing test reproduces it]
  D --> E[Fix the root cause and rerun]

notes.objective: Generate structured code review outputs including severity levels, affected line numbers, remediation guidance, and deployment impact assessments in JSON format.
notes.title: Structured review output in JSON
notes.gist: Machine-readable findings need a schema, validation against the diff and calibrated confidence, not prettier prose.
points: `claude -p` with `--output-format json` and `--json-schema` returns findings in `structured_output`: file, line, severity, category, remediation and deployment impact; check that the field exists before using it.
Schema-valid is not correct: add a validation layer that checks line numbers against the diff, applies severity rules and verifies that the cited code exists before comments are posted.
Include the pattern that triggered each finding and track how often developers dismiss each pattern, then refine or disable the noisy categories; measure precision and recall per category.
Per-field confidence scores with routing thresholds calibrated on a labeled set of reviewed changes send uncertain findings to human review; an overall accuracy figure hides weak categories.
Few-shot examples showing both flagged and unflagged cases, with the reason, define the decision boundary; putting existing tests in the prompt stops suggested test cases from duplicating coverage.
notes.tip: 'Output alternates between tables and bullets so the poster fails' means JSON schema output; 'accurate on average but wrong on one category' means precision and recall per category.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Diff] --> B[claude -p with json-schema]
  B --> C[Validate against diff metadata]
  C --> D{Confidence above threshold?}
  D -->|Yes| E[Post inline comment]
  D -->|No| F[Human review]

notes.objective: Develop refactoring agents that identify outdated patterns, suggest modernization replacements, and generate implementation code while managing dependencies across multiple services.
notes.title: Refactoring agents: plan, characterize, migrate
notes.gist: Plan large changes before editing, pin current behavior with tests, and move in small verified steps.
points: Plan mode (`--permission-mode plan` or Shift+Tab) explores and proposes without edits; use it for multi-file, architectural or unfamiliar-code changes and for dependencies across services, then switch to direct execution for the agreed steps.
Skip planning when the diff fits in one sentence (a typo, a log line, a rename): ask for the change directly and run the test.
With thin coverage, first write characterization tests that document existing behavior, then refactor in small testable increments and rerun the tests after each step.

Scale out safely: one subsystem per branch for reviewable pull requests, `/batch` or a `claude -p` loop with `--allowedTools` for many files, and `fork_session` to compare two modernization strategies from one baseline.
Record confirmed dependencies in a findings file, force the dependency scan as the first tool call with `tool_choice` in custom agents, and have a fresh Reviewer session check the Writer's result.
notes.tip: '380 files and reviewers must stay manageable' means one subsystem per branch with tests before review; 'unknown wrapper layers across 12 services' means plan mode first; 'rename a variable' means direct execution.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A{Change size and risk?} -->|One-sentence diff| B[Direct execution plus tests]
  A -->|Multi-file or unfamiliar| C[Plan mode and review the plan]
  C --> D[Characterization tests]
  D --> E[Small verified steps per branch]

cards.q: Where should a team's shared testing and error-handling conventions live so every clone gets them?
cards.a: In a committed CLAUDE.md at the repo root or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Personal style goes in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.

cards.q: How do you stop test-file guidance from loading for every task?
cards.a: Put it in `.claude/rules/testing.md` with `paths` globs matching test files; it loads only when matching files are in play.

cards.q: Where do committed custom slash commands and skills live?
cards.a: Commands in `.claude/commands/`, skills in `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. Commit them so CI and teammates get them; `~/.claude` is personal.

cards.q: Which skill frontmatter runs a workflow in an isolated subagent and limits its tools?
cards.a: `context: fork` for isolation and `allowed-tools` (for example Read Grep) for tools; `argument-hint` documents the arguments.

cards.q: Which exit code makes a Claude Code hook block an action, and what does exit 1 do?
cards.a: Exit 2 blocks, and stderr becomes the reason Claude sees. Exit 1 or any other non-zero code is a non-blocking error; the action still runs.

cards.q: How do you guarantee a linter runs after every file edit?
cards.a: A `PostToolUse` hook matching `Edit|Write` that runs the linter. A CLAUDE.md instruction is advisory and can be skipped.

cards.q: What is the settings precedence order, highest first?
cards.a: Managed settings, command-line `--settings`, project local, shared project, user. List keys such as `permissions.allow` merge across files.

cards.q: Which file holds personal project overrides that must stay out of git?
cards.a: `.claude/settings.local.json`. Shared team permissions and hooks go in the committed `.claude/settings.json`.

cards.q: How do you find every file that handles refunds in a large repository without filling the context?
cards.a: Glob with a name pattern such as `*refund*.yaml`, Grep exact strings, then Read only the matches; or delegate the search to an Explore subagent.

cards.q: When do you use plan mode, and when direct execution?
cards.a: Plan mode for multi-file, architectural or unfamiliar-code changes; direct execution when the change fits in one sentence, like a typo or rename.

cards.q: A production log shows a specific exception. What is the first move to find its cause?
cards.a: Grep the exact error string and the related handler names across the codebase, then Read the matching files and trace the callers.

cards.q: How do you run Claude Code in a CI job and get parseable findings?
cards.a: `claude -p` with `--output-format json` and `--json-schema`; read the `structured_output` field. `stream-json` gives event-by-event output.

cards.q: Which options reopen the previous Claude Code session, and how do you branch one?
cards.a: `claude --continue` reopens the most recent session and `--resume` picks one. Fork a session to branch it without changing the original.

cards.q: Why write characterization tests before refactoring a thin-coverage billing module?
cards.a: They record and lock in current behavior, so any behavior change introduced by automated edits shows up as a failing test.

cards.q: A refactor touches 380 files and reviewers need manageable pull requests. What do you do?
cards.a: Refactor one subsystem per branch, run its tests before review, and record dependencies and findings between steps.

summary.tests: Whether you can prove an LLM system works and find out why it does not: layered validation, eval design, segment-level measurement, graceful degradation, independent review and CI-friendly tests.
must_know: Schema-valid is not correct: add business-rule, cross-field and source cross-checks in code, retry with the specific errors, then quarantine or escalate.
Do arithmetic, counting and date math in application code, not in the model.
Start evals early with 20 to 50 tasks from real failures; grade with code first, LLM rubrics next and humans sparingly, using a different or stronger model as the judge.
Evaluate a prompt change on a held-out set that mirrors real inputs, one change at a time; a regression suite protects behavior that already worked.
Overall accuracy hides weak segments: use stratified sampling by document type, field and confidence, with per-category precision, recall and dismissal rates.
A fresh session reviews generated code and extractions; the session that wrote them is biased toward its own output.
Debug with full traces, `stop_reason`, `usage` and the `request-id`; temperature 0 is not deterministic, so assert structure or meaning in tests.
traps: Trusting one overall accuracy figure or high confidence scores instead of per-segment, stratified checks.
Letting the generating session or the same model grade its own work.
Rerunning a whole batch or failing a whole pipeline for a few bad items instead of isolating and retrying only the failures.

notes.objective: Implement validation layers that check extracted or generated output against business rules, JSON schemas, and domain-specific constraints to catch semantic errors that pass syntactic validation.
notes.title: Layered validation: shape, rules, meaning
notes.gist: Check shape first, then business rules and cross-references in code, then meaning with an independent reviewer.
points: Layer the checks: schema (types, required fields), then business rules (totals add up, dates in range, IDs exist), then cross-field and cross-document consistency, then a semantic review by a separate call or a person.

A schema-valid record can still be wrong: cross-check quoted passages and references against the source text, and verify line numbers, file paths and counts against the diff or database with deterministic code.
Compute in code: have Claude output the line items and do sums, conversions and date math in the application, because model arithmetic over long ledgers drifts by a few percent.

On failure retry with the original document, the failed output and the specific validation errors, cap the attempts, stop when the source lacks the data, then quarantine or escalate instead of silently dropping the record.

Make verification independent: the second request receives the source, the extraction and explicit discrepancy rules, not the first pass's reasoning, and a stronger model than the generator is a better judge.
notes.tip: 'Valid JSON but the totals are wrong' means business-rule validation in code; 'sums are off by 2 to 3 percent' means move arithmetic out of the model; 'self-review misses its own mistakes' means an independent reviewer.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Model output] --> B{Schema valid?}
  B -->|No| F[Retry with errors fed back]
  B -->|Yes| C{Rules and cross-checks pass?}
  C -->|No| F
  C -->|Yes| D[Independent semantic review]
  D --> E[Load into the backend]

notes.objective: Design and execute evaluation methodologies to measure accuracy, identify failure patterns, and audit system performance across diverse document types and use cases.
notes.title: Build evals: criteria, tasks, graders
notes.gist: Write measurable criteria, collect realistic balanced tasks, and grade with the cheapest reliable method.
points: Success criteria must be specific and measurable (F1 of at least 0.85 on a held-out set, 99.5% non-toxic outputs, 95% of responses under 200 ms); one metric rarely covers fidelity, consistency, tone, safety and latency.

Start early and small: 20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures and manual checks beat waiting for hundreds; each task is unambiguous (two experts would agree on pass or fail) with a reference solution, and a 0% pass rate on many trials usually means a broken task.
Balance the set with cases where a behavior should and should not occur plus edge cases (irrelevant, very long, ambiguous input), and run every trial from a clean, identical environment.

Grade with code first (exact or string match, unit tests: fast and reliable), then LLM graders with a clear rubric and an 'Unknown' option, calibrated against humans, one judge per dimension and a different or stronger model than the generator; humans sparingly. Grade the outcome, not the path, and give partial credit.

Capability evals start at a low pass rate as a hill to climb, regression evals sit near 100% to protect existing behavior; run several trials (pass@k is at least one success, pass^k all k succeed: 75% per trial gives about 42% for three) and read transcripts to check the graders are fair.
notes.tip: 'A prompt change looks better on five examples' needs a held-out set that mirrors real inputs and defined criteria; 'the same model grades its own output' is a flaw; 'a fix broke another behavior' is what a regression suite catches.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Real failures and manual checks] --> B[Clear tasks with reference answers]
  B --> C[Run in a clean environment]
  C --> D[Grade: code, LLM rubric, human]
  D --> E[Read transcripts, fix tasks or agent]

notes.objective: Design and execute evaluation methodologies to measure accuracy, identify failure patterns, and audit system performance across diverse document types and use cases.
notes.title: Measure by segment, not just overall
notes.gist: An average hides weak document types and fields, so sample, segment and calibrate before reducing human review.
points: Overall accuracy (for example 97.4%) hides weak segments: break it down by document type, field and source before automating anything, and set a validated threshold per segment.

Sample high-confidence outputs too: stratified random sampling across document type, source and section finds errors that the confidence score misses, and error rates are monitored inside each stratum.
Add a category or pattern field to every flagged item and track approval or dismissal rates by it; a category with high dismissal is paused or refined, not the whole system.
Calibrate confidence: produce per-field confidence scores, set routing thresholds per field on labeled pilot data, and send low-confidence fields to reviewers.

Pilot on a representative, diverse batch before the full run, analyze validation failures and missing-field patterns, refine the prompt, then scale; report precision and recall per category, not one blended number.
notes.tip: '99% schema compliance and high confidence yet errors reach customers' means stratified sampling and per-segment accuracy; 'developers dismiss one kind of comment' means track dismissal by category.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Pilot batch with mixed document types] --> B[Accuracy per type and field]
  B --> C{Segment meets its threshold?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Automate that segment]
  C -->|No| E[Keep review and refine the prompt]

notes.objective: Build error handling and graceful degradation mechanisms that allow systems to process incomplete or malformed inputs without failing entirely.
notes.title: Graceful degradation for bad inputs
notes.gist: Isolate failures per item, return partial results with context, and retry only what can succeed.
points: A failing worker returns partial results with context: section ID, failure category, what it retrieved, the queries tried and suggested recovery, so the coordinator can retry, reassign or proceed without it.

Handle each item on its own: in a batch one failed request never affects the others, so retry only the `errored` or `expired` custom_ids and keep the succeeded results instead of rerunning everything.

Match the response to the cause: `max_tokens` truncation means raise the limit or stream, an oversized payload (413) means shrink before resubmitting, `invalid_request_error` means fix the request, and 429, 5xx or 529 mean backoff with `retry-after`.

Tell the agent when a tool is failing so it can adapt, and pair that with deterministic safeguards (retry logic, checkpoints) and resumable state so an error resumes where the agent stopped instead of restarting.

Categorize bad input explicitly: legitimately absent optional data becomes null, unreadable required data is retried or escalated, and corrupted documents go to human review, each with rules and examples.
notes.tip: 'One bad document fails the whole run' means isolate failures and return structured partial results; 'the whole batch is rerun for three failures' means retry only the failed custom_ids.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Item fails] --> B{Failure cause?}
  B -->|Transient| C[Backoff and retry]
  B -->|Bad or missing data| D[Mark incomplete with a reason]
  B -->|Unreadable| E[Human review queue]
  C --> F[Continue with the other items]
  D --> F
  E --> F

notes.objective: Construct multi-agent architectures that route tasks to specialized Claude agents and aggregate their outputs while maintaining consistency and quality.
notes.title: Multi-agent consistency and quality control
notes.gist: Keep the coordinator in control, validate in two phases and keep conflicts visible through synthesis.
points: Route by specialty through a coordinator that keeps control: follow-ups, error handling and recovery all pass through it rather than between workers.

Validate in two phases: granular checks on each paper or section first, then a unified cross-item consistency review before synthesis; independent per-section reviewers plus an integration reviewer catch cross-section contradictions.
A coordinator validation loop assesses synthesis completeness, issues targeted redelegations for the gaps and reruns until the quality bar is met.
Keep conflicts visible: retain both projections with full source attribution and a transparency note instead of averaging or picking one; workers return structured claim-and-evidence records.

Start the synthesis prompt with a structured index of findings and organize details into labeled subsections, because long mixed context buries findings; judge agents by end state with a rubric (accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, efficiency).
notes.tip: 'The final report mixes contradictory statistics' means preserve both with attribution; 'quality drops when many findings are pasted together' means an index first and labeled sections; 'an agent took a different valid path' means grade the end state.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Coordinator routes to specialists] --> B[Per-item quality checks]
  B --> C[Cross-item consistency review]
  C --> D{Complete and consistent?}
  D -->|No| E[Redelegate the gaps]
  D -->|Yes| F[Final synthesis]

notes.objective: Identify and address systematic gaps in AI-generated code by analyzing reviewer feedback, test failures, and domain-specific requirements to improve generation quality.
notes.title: Closing systematic gaps in generated code
notes.gist: Group reviewer feedback and failures into patterns, then fix the cause with tests, rules and an independent check.
points: Mine the feedback for patterns: add an `issue_category` field to review findings and measure approval or dismissal by category and module or contract type; recurring categories are systematic gaps.

Write tests first (expected behavior, edge cases, performance) or build a reference suite, have Claude generate code, and iterate on specific failures: failing test names, inputs, expected versus actual output and stack traces.
Review in a fresh session that sees only the diff, repository context and guidelines; a same-session review is biased toward the code and reasoning it just produced.

Encode the missing domain knowledge: standards, high-value test criteria and fixtures in a shared CLAUDE.md or rule file, and have Claude ask engineers targeted questions (tenant isolation, observability conventions, exception handling) before generating.
Verify in the real environment before the agent declares success, and add runtime checks such as allowing `approve_invoice` only after `validate_invoice` has passed for that invoice.
notes.tip: 'Generated code compiles but reviewers keep finding the same omissions' means encode the conventions and questions the generator lacked; 'the same session reviews its own code' means a fresh reviewer session.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Reviewer feedback and test failures] --> B[Group by category]
  B --> C[Add tests, rules or examples]
  C --> D[Regenerate in a clean session]
  D --> E[Independent review and a real run]

notes.objective: Integrate Claude into CI/CD pipelines and automated workflows using the Claude Agent SDK, including session management and tool integration for code generation and review tasks.
notes.title: Claude in CI: sessions and test strategy
notes.gist: Run Claude from the pipeline with capped cost and test the surrounding system with fixtures, simulations and gates.
points: `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` takes `anthropic_api_key` from secrets and `claude_args` such as `--max-turns`, `--model` and `--allowedTools`; automation mode runs a `prompt` with nobody present; grant minimal permissions and set workflow timeouts and concurrency limits to cap cost.

In scripts `claude -p --output-format json` returns a `session_id`; continue with `--resume <id>` or `--continue`, and in the Agent SDK use `resume` and `fork_session`; session files are local, so ephemeral CI hosts need a session store or the needed state passed into a fresh prompt.

Integration-testing an LLM feature: cache and replay real responses as fixtures for routine runs, keep a small live set for merges to main, and assert structure or semantic equivalence because temperature 0 does not give identical text.

Test agents against simulated services that replay scripted success and failure scenarios, keep a regression suite, and roll prompt or model changes out to a fraction of traffic while watching quality metrics.
Keep prompts and model versions in version control with review and tagged releases, so every change has an author and a history, and run the eval suite on each change as a gate.
notes.tip: 'Flaky assertions at temperature 0' means structural or semantic assertions instead of exact strings; 'nobody can tell what changed in the prompt' means version control and CI gates; 'an agent only ever tested against live services' means scripted simulations.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Pull request] --> B[Action runs claude with a prompt]
  B --> C[Eval suite and fixture replay]
  C --> D{Gates pass?}
  D -->|Yes| E[Merge and staged rollout]
  D -->|No| F[Block with a report]

notes.objective: Design and execute evaluation methodologies to measure accuracy, identify failure patterns, and audit system performance across diverse document types and use cases.
notes.title: Debug with traces, IDs and stop reasons
notes.gist: Capture every step of a run so you can locate the defect by stage instead of guessing.
points: Log every turn of a multi-step agent (each model response, tool call and result); 'it is not finding obvious information' stays invisible without a trace that shows bad queries, poor sources or tool failures.

Locate the defect by stage: if answers faithfully follow the supplied documents but those documents are wrong, the retrieval layer is at fault; if retrieval is right and the answer is wrong, inspect the assembled prompt and the model response.

Read `stop_reason` first for truncated JSON or abrupt endings (`max_tokens`), read `usage` for real token cost, and quote the `request-id` response header when asking Anthropic support about a specific request.
When several changes ship together, isolate each one against a fixed benchmark; temperature 0 is not deterministic, so compare pass rates over several trials rather than single outputs.
Monitor production: record usage and stop reasons per call, alert on anomalous error or rate-limit patterns, and give each session a token counter and a step ceiling so runaway retry loops stop.
notes.tip: 'Wrong answers although the model follows its documents faithfully' is a retrieval defect; 'intermittent 5xx cannot be reproduced' means capture the request-id; 'a sudden cost spike' means check `usage` and loop ceilings.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Wrong or odd output] --> B[Read the trace]
  B --> C{Where does it go wrong?}
  C -->|Retrieved documents| D[Fix search or indexing]
  C -->|Prompt or model step| E[Fix the prompt, one change at a time]
  C -->|Output cut off| F[Check stop_reason and max_tokens]

cards.q: An extraction returns valid JSON with an incorrect invoice total. Which layer catches it?
cards.a: A business-rule check in your own code (line items sum to the total), after the schema check. Schema validation alone cannot catch wrong values.

cards.q: Model-computed sums over a long ledger are off by 2 to 3 percent. What is the fix?
cards.a: Have Claude output the line items and do summation and other arithmetic in application code, where it is exact.

cards.q: How do you retry a failed extraction effectively?
cards.a: Send the original document, the failed output and the specific validation errors for a targeted correction, cap the attempts, then escalate.

cards.q: How many tasks do you need to start an eval, and where do they come from?
cards.a: Roughly 20 to 50 small tasks taken from real failures and manual checks; each needs a clear pass or fail.

cards.q: Which grading method comes first, and when do you use an LLM grader?
cards.a: Code-based grading (exact match, tests) first: fastest and most reliable. LLM graders with a clear rubric for judgments code cannot make; humans sparingly.

cards.q: Why should the grader model differ from the generating model?
cards.a: The same model shares its blind spots and tends to favor its own output; use a different or stronger model and calibrate it against humans.

cards.q: What is the difference between capability evals and regression evals?
cards.a: Capability evals start at a low pass rate as a hill to climb; regression evals sit near 100% and protect behavior that already worked.

cards.q: A prompt change improved the five examples you tried. What must happen before it ships?
cards.a: Evaluate it on a held-out set that reflects real inputs against defined criteria, one change at a time, ideally with a staged rollout.

cards.q: Overall extraction accuracy is 97.4 percent. Why not cut human review?
cards.a: Averages hide weak segments. Break accuracy down by document type and field, and automate only segments that meet validated thresholds.

cards.q: How do you catch errors that high confidence scores hide?
cards.a: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence outputs across document type, source and field, monitoring error rates inside each stratum.

cards.q: Developers dismiss most review comments of one kind. How do you find the cause?
cards.a: Add a category or pattern field to each finding, track dismissal rates by it, and refine or disable the noisy category.

cards.q: A batch of 18,000 requests finishes with a few errors. What do you rerun?
cards.a: Only the `errored` and `expired` custom_ids; keep and apply the succeeded results. One failed request never affects the rest.

cards.q: Why review generated code in a fresh session?
cards.a: It sees only the diff, repo context and guidelines, so it is not biased toward the code and reasoning of the session that wrote it.

cards.q: Temperature is 0 yet exact-string test assertions still fail. What do you change?
cards.a: Assert structure and semantic equivalence instead of exact text, replay cached responses for routine runs, and keep a small live set for merges.

cards.q: Users report wrong answers, but traces show Claude follows the supplied documents faithfully. Where is the defect?
cards.a: In the retrieval layer that selects the documents; fix search or indexing, not the prompt or the model.
